A.io: Discuss the use of lipid testing for cardiovascular risk assessment
A.q: A 55-year-old's lipid values are entered into a cardiovascular risk equation. What does that step produce?
opts: A diagnosis of acute infarction
A risk equation estimates future risk; acute infarction is diagnosed with troponin and the clinical picture.
A 10-year risk estimate

Correct. Lipid values feed 10-year risk estimation, with the PREVENT (Predicting Risk of cardiovascular disease EVENTs) equations in the current guideline, and the estimate then drives treatment intensity.
A measured LDL-C value
LDL-C (low-density lipoprotein cholesterol) is an input, usually calculated; the equation's output is risk.
A lifetime lipoprotein(a) level
Lipoprotein(a) is measured once in the lab; it is not produced by a risk equation.

A.io: Compare and contrast cardiac biomarkers: Creatine kinase, Cardiac troponins, BNP, hs-CRP
A.q: A 55-year-old presents two days after an episode of chest pain. Why is troponin preferred over CK-MB (creatine kinase muscle-brain isoenzyme)?
opts: It rises later and clears more quickly
The reverse: troponin rises sooner and remains elevated longer than CK-MB.
It is also raised by skeletal muscle injury
Lack of cardiac specificity is creatine kinase's weakness. Troponin has very high specificity for myocardial injury.
It is cheaper and needs no clinical context
Cost is not the stated advantage, and troponin always needs clinical context; a single value out of context is a classic trap.
It rises sooner and stays elevated longer
Correct. That expands the window for diagnosis and treatment, which matters for a patient presenting late.

A.io: Identify common abnormal cardiovascular imaging findings
A.q: What is cephalization on a chest radiograph?
opts: Fluid tracking into the interlobar fissures
That would be described as effusion or fissural fluid rather than cephalization.
The trachea deviating toward the apex
Tracheal deviation is a different sign entirely. Cephalization is enlargement of the upper zone vessels.
Upper zone vessels becoming larger
Correct. Flow redistributes upward, which is why the sign sits in the lungs while the problem is in the heart.
Calcification of the aortic arch
Great vessel calcification is listed separately from cephalization.

A.io: Discuss indications for ordering a lipid profile
A.q: A 35-year-old has lipoprotein(a) measured for the first time. How often does it generally need measuring?
opts: Every year
Annual repetition adds nothing for a value that is largely genetic and stable across life.
Every 5 years
Five-yearly repetition is the adult screening interval for the standard lipid panel, not for lipoprotein(a).
Once in a lifetime
Correct. It is more than 90% genetically determined and stable over life, and needs no fasting, so a single measurement generally suffices.
After every statin change
Statins do not lower lipoprotein(a), so rechecking it with each statin change would not guide therapy.

A.io: Define absolute and relative refractory periods
A.q: What distinguishes the relative from the absolute refractory period?
opts: In the relative period no stimulus of any strength will produce a response
That describes the absolute period; the relative one can be overcome.
In the relative period a sufficiently strong stimulus can produce a response
Correct. It is the dangerous window: the cell is excitable again but not yet fully recovered, so a stimulus arriving there can start something abnormal.
The relative period occurs before the absolute period
It runs from the middle to the end of phase three, after the absolute period.
The relative period occupies the whole of phase 4
Phase four is the resting state, in which the cell responds normally.

A.io: Analyze a lipid profile
A.q: A 44-year-old asks what the normal LDL-C (low-density lipoprotein cholesterol) is. What is the accurate answer?
opts: Below 200 mg/dL for everyone
Below 200 mg/dL is the desirable total cholesterol, not an LDL-C goal, and LDL-C goals vary by risk.
Below 150 mg/dL for everyone
Below 150 mg/dL is the desirable triglyceride level; LDL-C has risk-based goals instead.
The goal depends on her risk tier

Correct. Adult LDL-C and non-HDL-C have no single normal value; the goal depends on the patient's atherosclerotic risk tier, whereas triglyceride, apoB (apolipoprotein B) and lipoprotein(a) thresholds are more fixed.
Any value while HDL-C is high
A high HDL-C (high-density lipoprotein cholesterol) does not cancel LDL-C; HDL-C is not even a treatment target.

A.io: Measure the cardiothoracic ratio to evaluate cardiac enlargement
A.q: A properly performed posteroanterior chest radiograph shows the cardiac silhouette occupying 58 percent of the internal thoracic diameter. What does that suggest?
opts: A normal heart size
A normal ratio sits below about one half of the internal thoracic diameter, and this measurement is above it.
Pulmonary hypertension without cardiac enlargement
The ratio measures the cardiac silhouette rather than the pulmonary circulation.
Cardiomegaly
Correct. The silhouette should normally occupy no more than about half the internal thoracic diameter, so this exceeds it.
A pericardial effusion specifically
An effusion can enlarge the silhouette, but the ratio identifies enlargement rather than its cause.

A.io: Discuss indications, advantages, and limitations of cardiac MRI
A.q: What does cardiovascular magnetic resonance map to build its three-dimensional images?
opts: Iodinated contrast pooling in vessels
Magnetic resonance needs no iodinated contrast, which is one of its advantages; the image comes from hydrogen atoms in the tissue itself.
Reflected high-frequency sound pulses
Reflected sound forms an ultrasound or echocardiographic image; magnetic resonance maps hydrogen atoms using magnetic fields and radiofrequency.
Gamma rays emitted by an injected tracer
Gamma emission from a radioactive tracer forms a nuclear perfusion image; magnetic resonance uses no radioactive tracer and no ionizing radiation, only hydrogen atoms in the tissue.
Hydrogen atoms
Correct. Strong magnetic fields and radiofrequency pulses are used to map hydrogen atoms, giving very detailed anatomy of the heart and great vessels.

A.io: Discuss indications, advantages, and limitations of nuclear cardiology studies
A.q: How is the heart stressed for a nuclear perfusion study in a patient who cannot exercise?
opts: Pharmacologically, with an agent such as adenosine
Correct. The stress can be produced by exercise or by drug, and the imaging is the same either way.
By transesophageal pacing
Pacing is not the described method; pharmacological stress with an agent such as adenosine is.
By cold pressor testing
Not among the described methods. Pharmacological stress, with an agent such as adenosine, is used instead.
The study cannot be performed without exercise
Pharmacological stress exists precisely so that it can be performed without exercise.

A.io: Measure the cardiothoracic ratio to evaluate cardiac enlargement
A.q: Why does the cardiothoracic ratio require a properly performed posteroanterior film?
opts: Only a posteroanterior film shows the pulmonary vasculature
Vasculature is visible on other projections; it is the silhouette measurement that depends on projection.
Projection alters the apparent size of the cardiac silhouette
Correct. A ratio measured off the wrong projection is a measurement of the technique rather than of the heart.
Contrast is required and is only given for posteroanterior films
No contrast is involved in measuring the ratio; it is the projection that alters the apparent silhouette size.
The ratio can only be calculated with electrocardiographic gating
Gating belongs to cardiac computed tomography rather than to plain radiography.

A.io: Determine heart rate using an electrocardiogram
A.q: Which relationship is checked when assessing P waves on a strip?
opts: Whether there is a P wave for every QRS complex and a QRS for every P wave
Correct. It is a two-way check, and each direction fails in a different way, which is what makes the blocks distinguishable.
Whether the P wave is taller than the T wave
Relative amplitude is not the check; it is whether each P has a QRS and each QRS a P.
Whether the P wave falls within the QT interval
The QT interval covers ventricular activity and does not contain the P wave.
Whether the P wave is visible in all twelve leads
The described check concerns the relationship with the QRS rather than visibility across leads.

A.io: Describe action potentials and impulse conduction through the cardiac conduction system
A.q: What is the ionic arrangement during phase 4, the resting state?
opts: More sodium inside the cell, with potassium outside
The arrangement is the other way round: potassium is the ion held inside at rest.
Equal concentrations of all ions across the membrane
An equal distribution would leave no voltage across the membrane, and the resting cell holds a substantial one.
Calcium inside the cell with potassium outside
Calcium sits outside at rest and enters later, during the plateau.
More potassium inside the cell
Correct. That separation is the stored charge the cell spends when it fires, and restoring it is what the later phases achieve. With sodium and calcium outside.

A.io: Discuss indications, advantages, and limitations of cardiac CT
A.q: Which is an indication for cardiac computed tomography rather than the angiographic study?
opts: Detecting and excluding coronary stenosis
Stenosis detection is the indication for the angiographic study.
Assessing exercise capacity
Exercise capacity is assessed by stress testing rather than by cardiac computed tomography.
Evaluating deep venous thrombosis
Deep vein thrombosis is assessed by vascular ultrasound rather than by cardiac computed tomography.
Pre-operative planning before cardiac surgery

Correct, alongside calcium deposits, coronary anatomical anomalies and congenital disease, and it is usually done immediately before the angiographic study. Particularly valvular and great vessel procedures.

A.io: Discuss indications, advantages, and limitations of stress testing
A.q: What is the echocardiogram looking for after exercise, and why must it be obtained quickly?
opts: Valve gradients, which take time to develop
The study looks for induced wall motion abnormality rather than valve gradients.
Pericardial fluid, which accumulates after exertion
Pericardial fluid is not what the post-exercise images are looking for.
Coronary calcium, which is best seen at high heart rates
Calcium is assessed by computed tomography and is unrelated to heart rate.
Abnormal left ventricular wall motion induced by exercise
Correct. The finding is transient, so the patient is asked to dismount quickly and the heart is imaged before it settles. Which resolves as the heart recovers.

A.io: Discuss indications for ordering coagulation studies
A.q: A 72-year-old woman takes a direct oral anticoagulant and has a normal prothrombin time and partial thromboplastin time. What does this mean for her bleeding risk?
opts: Bleeding risk is excluded
Normal screening times do not remove the bleeding risk from these drugs.
Routine level monitoring is required
Routine monitoring of direct oral anticoagulants is not required.
The drug has no anticoagulant effect
These drugs can be fully active while leaving the prothrombin time and partial thromboplastin time normal.
Bleeding risk is still increased
Correct. Most direct oral anticoagulants may not derange the prothrombin time or partial thromboplastin time yet still increase bleeding risk, and routine monitoring is not required.

A.io: Compare and contrast laboratory studies used to evaluate bleeding and thrombotic disorders
A.q: A 29-year-old woman with recurrent thrombosis is evaluated for a hypercoagulable state. Which deficiency is a primary cause tested?
opts: Hemophilia A
Hemophilia A is a clotting factor deficiency that causes bleeding, not a hypercoagulable state.
Protein C deficiency
Correct. Primary hypercoagulable causes include deficiencies of antithrombin III, protein C and protein S, along with abnormal fibrinolytic mechanisms.
Immune thrombocytopenia
Immune thrombocytopenia lowers the platelet count, a bleeding problem.
Factor VII deficiency
Factor VII deficiency impairs clotting and causes bleeding, so it is not a hypercoagulable cause.

A.io: Compare and contrast lipids and lipoproteins involved in atherosclerotic disease
A.q: A 48-year-old asks why cholesterol travels in the blood inside particles. What is the reason?
opts: Cholesterol and triglycerides are insoluble
Correct. The major lipids, cholesterol and triglycerides, are insoluble in plasma, so they travel packaged inside lipoproteins.
Cholesterol is broken down by plasma enzymes
The reason is solubility, not protection from enzymes; lipoprotein lipase acts on triglycerides carried in the particles.
Particles let the kidney filter cholesterol
Lipoproteins are not a route for renal filtration; LDL (low-density lipoprotein) is cleared by receptors on hepatocytes.
Free cholesterol would raise the troponin
Troponin is a myocyte injury marker and has nothing to do with how lipids are carried.

A.io: Compare and contrast laboratory studies used to evaluate bleeding and thrombotic disorders
A.q: A 36-year-old woman has easy bruising and bleeding gums. Which initial set of studies is appropriate?
opts: Prothrombin time, activated partial thromboplastin time and D-dimer
That is the thrombotic workup. A bleeding patient needs the platelet count and smear and fibrinogen instead of D-dimer.
D-dimer and fibrin monomers only
These markers of clot formation and breakdown do not screen platelets or coagulation factors.
Blood count with smear, clotting times and fibrinogen
Correct. The bleeding workup is a blood count with differential and peripheral smear, prothrombin time with international normalized ratio, activated partial thromboplastin time and fibrinogen.
Bleeding time alone
One test cannot screen every cause of bleeding, and platelets, factors and fibrinogen all need evaluating.

A.io: Measure and interpret the intervals, segments and waves of the cardiac cycle
A.q: What must a deflection do to count as a true S wave?
opts: Follow the T wave
The S wave follows the R wave, well before the T wave; what defines it is crossing the baseline.
Exceed one small box in amplitude
The defining requirement is crossing the baseline rather than reaching an amplitude.
Extend below the baseline
Correct. If it does not, it is called an S wave pattern instead, which is a distinction of naming that matters when describing a tracing precisely.
Appear in every lead
Not all three QRS waves are present in every lead or every rhythm.

A.io: Describe the fundamental principles of electrocardiography
A.q: Lead I and lead aVL form a contiguous group with which other leads?
opts: V5 and V6
Correct. Leads I, aVL, V5 and V6 look at the same area of the heart, so a change across all four means more than one isolated lead.
V1 and V2
V1 and V2 sit in the group with V3 and V4, which looks at a different area; leads I and aVL group with V5 and V6.
II and III
Leads II and III group with aVF; leads I and aVL group with V5 and V6.
V3 and V4
V3 and V4 belong to the V1 to V4 group rather than the lead I group; leads I and aVL group with V5 and V6.

A.io: Describe action potentials and impulse conduction through the cardiac conduction system
A.q: Which structure is described as the third pacemaker, taking over if both the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes fail?
opts: The bundle of His
The bundle of His is the connection between the atrioventricular node and the bundle branches rather than the third pacemaker.
The left anterior fascicle
The fascicles are branches of the conducting pathway rather than a named pacemaker.
The Purkinje network
Correct, at an intrinsic rate of twenty to forty -- slow enough to be a last resort rather than a comfortable substitute.
The internodal tracts
These connect the sinoatrial node to the atrioventricular node rather than pacing the heart.

A.io: Discuss indications, advantages, and limitations of cardiac MRI
A.q: Which aortic conditions is cardiovascular magnetic resonance used to diagnose and monitor?
opts: The coronary artery calcium burden
Calcium is scored by non-contrast computed tomography rather than by magnetic resonance.
Aneurysm, dissection, hematoma, coarctation
Correct. All four are questions about the wall and the lumen of a large vessel, which is where its detailed anatomy is most useful.
Valve vegetations
Vegetations are sought on echocardiography, particularly the transesophageal study.
Deep venous thrombosis
Deep vein thrombosis is assessed by vascular ultrasound rather than by cardiovascular magnetic resonance.
A.cite: Cardiac Imaging and Vascular Studies - Elwaya.pptx, Slide 56

A.io: Describe laboratory findings associated with platelet abnormalities
A.q: A 19-year-old woman has heavy menses and easy bruising. Which inherited bleeding disorder is the most common overall?
opts: Hemophilia A
Hemophilia A, factor VIII deficiency, is common among the factor deficiencies, but von Willebrand disease is the most common inherited bleeding disorder overall.
Hemophilia B
Hemophilia B, factor IX deficiency, is less common than von Willebrand disease.
Factor XIII deficiency
Factor XIII deficiency is rare, marked by umbilical stump bleeding and lifelong severe bleeding, and far less common than von Willebrand disease.
von Willebrand disease
Correct. von Willebrand disease is the most common inherited bleeding disorder, and it is tested with von Willebrand factor antigen, activity and a factor VIII level.

A.io: Describe the fundamental principles of electrocardiography
A.q: On standard calibration, a deflection rises ten millimeters, which is two large boxes. What voltage does it represent?
opts: 1 millivolt
Correct. Standard calibration sets two large boxes, a 10 millimeter deflection, equal to 1 millivolt, so each small box is 0.1 millivolt.
10 millivolts
That is ten times too large; on standard calibration a 10 millimeter deflection equals 1 millivolt, because each small box is 0.1 millivolt.
0.1 millivolt
That is the value of a single small box, one millimeter tall; two large boxes equal 10 millimeters, which is 1 millivolt.
0.5 millivolt
That would be half the standard deflection; a rise of two large boxes, 10 millimeters, equals 1 millivolt.

A.io: Describe action potentials and impulse conduction through the cardiac conduction system
A.q: What happens during phase 0, the upstroke?
opts: Calcium channels open and calcium enters the cell
Calcium entry belongs to phase two, the plateau, and it is what triggers contraction.
Fast sodium channels open and sodium rushes into the cell
Correct. It is the fastest event in the cycle, and the rapid inward sodium current is what drives the voltage positive.
Potassium channels open and potassium leaves the cell
Potassium movement dominates the repolarizing phases rather than the upstroke.
Sodium is actively pumped out of the cell
Active extrusion restores the gradient over time; the upstroke is a passive rapid influx.

A.io: Compare and contrast cardiovascular imaging modalities
A.q: Which limitations are described for vascular ultrasound?
opts: Ionizing radiation dose and contrast nephrotoxicity
Neither applies: ultrasound uses no ionizing radiation and no iodinated contrast.
Highly operator dependent, limited by body habitus
Correct. Calcification causes acoustic shadowing, which matters because the vessels most worth imaging are often the ones most calcified. Degraded by bone, air and calcification.
Dependence on heart rate and rhythm
Rate and rhythm dependence belongs to cardiac computed tomography.
Inability to show blood flow
Showing both anatomy and flow is one of its advantages rather than a limitation, with Doppler supplying the flow.
A.cite: Cardiac Imaging and Vascular Studies - Elwaya.pptx, Slide 18

A.io: Define: hemostasis, primary hemostasis, secondary hemostasis, thrombus, fibrinolysis, fibrin degradation products, D-dimer
A.q: A 40-year-old man has a D-dimer reported. Which three enzymes act to form this cross-linked fibrin degradation product?
opts: Thrombin, tissue factor and factor VII
Tissue factor and factor VII start the extrinsic pathway. They help generate thrombin, but they do not degrade cross-linked fibrin into D-dimer.
Plasmin, antithrombin and protein C
Antithrombin and protein C are anticoagulant proteins that restrain clotting. D-dimer requires thrombin, factor XIII and plasmin.
Factor Xa, factor IXa and factor VIIIa
These are coagulation factors in the generation of thrombin. None of them cross-links or degrades fibrin to make D-dimer.
Thrombin, factor XIII and plasmin
Correct. D-dimer results from the action of thrombin (forming fibrin), activated factor XIII (cross-linking it) and plasmin (degrading it).

A.io: Describe measured and calculated lipid profile components
A.q: A 50-year-old man gets a standard lipid panel. Which components are measured directly?
opts: LDL-C, non-HDL-C and triglycerides
LDL-C and non-HDL-C are both calculated from the measured values, not measured directly on a standard panel.
Total cholesterol, HDL-C and triglycerides

Correct. Those three are measured. LDL-C (low-density lipoprotein cholesterol) and non-HDL-C are calculated, so the LDL-C on a standard report is an estimate. HDL-C is high-density lipoprotein cholesterol.
Total cholesterol, LDL-C and non-HDL-C
Total cholesterol is measured, but LDL-C and non-HDL-C are calculated.
LDL-C, HDL-C and total cholesterol
LDL-C is the classic calculated value; on a standard panel it is an estimate rather than a measurement.

A.io: Compare and contrast lipids and lipoproteins involved in atherosclerotic disease
A.q: A 39-year-old is found to have a variant of an apolipoprotein that is critical in triglyceride clearance. Which apolipoprotein is that?
opts: ApoA-II (apolipoprotein A-II)
ApoA-II is the second most abundant HDL (high-density lipoprotein) apolipoprotein, not the triglyceride-clearance protein.
ApoB-48 (apolipoprotein B-48)
ApoB-48 is the structural protein of chylomicrons, made by the intestine.
ApoE (apolipoprotein E)
Correct. ApoE is important in triglyceride metabolism and critical in triglyceride clearance. ApoC, apoC-III and apoA-V regulate triglyceride metabolism.
Apo(a) (apolipoprotein(a))
Apo(a) forms lipoprotein(a); its significance is atherogenic and genetic risk rather than triglyceride clearance.

A.io: Describe laboratory findings associated with platelet abnormalities
A.q: A 70-year-old man bleeds, and a physician reviews platelet counts. Which statement about count and bleeding is correct?
opts: Only low counts cause bleeding
Extreme thrombocythemia can also cause bleeding, so a very high count does not protect against it.
Only high counts cause bleeding
Thrombocytopenia clearly causes bleeding, with risk rising as the count falls.
Counts never cause bleeding with a normal prothrombin time
A normal prothrombin time and partial thromboplastin time with bleeding actually points toward a platelet problem, quantitative or qualitative.
Very low and very high counts can both cause bleeding
Correct. Thrombocytopenia and extreme thrombocythemia, above 1,000 times 10 to the ninth per liter, can both cause bleeding.

A.io: Discuss diagnostic testing for: primary hemostasis, secondary hemostasis, fibrinolysis
A.q: A 50-year-old man has an isolated prolonged partial thromboplastin time. Before further evaluation, which effect must be ruled out first?
opts: Heparin
Correct. The algorithm for an isolated prolonged partial thromboplastin time begins by ruling out heparin effect.
Warfarin
Warfarin mainly prolongs the prothrombin time and international normalized ratio.
Aspirin
Aspirin affects platelet function and leaves the partial thromboplastin time normal.
Platelet clumping
Clumping falsely lowers the automated platelet count. It does not prolong the partial thromboplastin time.

A.io: Describe laboratory findings associated with platelet abnormalities
A.q: A 52-year-old man has a low automated platelet count. His smear shows platelet clumps and platelets surrounding neutrophils. What does this indicate?
opts: Disseminated intravascular coagulation
Disseminated intravascular coagulation shows a low count with prolonged clotting times, low fibrinogen and a high D-dimer, not clumping on the smear.
Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura shows fragmented red cells (schistocytes) on the smear, not platelet clumps.
A falsely low count
Correct. Clumping and platelets ringing neutrophils (satellitism) make the automated count read falsely low, which is spurious thrombocytopenia.
Immune thrombocytopenia
A true immune thrombocytopenia has few platelets on the smear. Clumping means the platelets are present but miscounted.

A.io: Discuss indications for ordering cardiac biomarkers
A.q: A 64-year-old has an acute coronary syndrome confirmed. Besides troponin, which biomarker also carries prognostic value after the event?
opts: Creatine kinase
Creatine kinase is largely historical for infarction and is used for skeletal muscle injury, not prognosis after acute coronary syndrome.
Myoglobin
Myoglobin is among the markers no longer used to evaluate cardiac disease.
Lactate dehydrogenase
Lactate dehydrogenase is also retired from cardiac evaluation.
B-type natriuretic peptide
Correct. B-type natriuretic peptide or its N-terminal fragment supports heart failure diagnosis and triage and is also prognostic after acute coronary syndrome.

A.io: Measure and interpret the intervals, segments and waves of the cardiac cycle
A.q: What does the QRS complex represent, and what should it look like?
opts: Ventricular repolarization, broad and rounded
Ventricular repolarization is the T wave, which is broad and rounded.
Ventricular depolarization, narrow with sharp points
Correct, with a duration under three small boxes. A wide QRS means the ventricles were not activated through the normal fast pathway.
Atrial depolarization, narrow and upright
Atrial depolarization is the P wave rather than the QRS complex, which is ventricular.
The plateau phase of the action potential
The plateau corresponds to the ST segment rather than to the QRS.

A.io: Identify the standard limb and precordial leads and their proper anatomical placement
A.q: What is the hexaxial reference system used to determine?
opts: The normal axis of the heart
Correct. Six views in one plane are what make an axis calculable at all.
The heart rate
Rate is determined from the strip by the six-second or three hundred method rather than from the axis system.
The horizontal view of the heart
The horizontal view comes from the precordial leads; the hexaxial system determines the axis.
The duration of the QT interval
Interval durations are measured on the tracing rather than derived from the reference system.

A.io: Discuss indications for ordering cardiac biomarkers
A.q: A 50-year-old in primary prevention has borderline cardiovascular risk. When is high-sensitivity C-reactive protein appropriate?
opts: To refine atherosclerotic risk
Correct. It is an inflammatory risk-enhancing marker in select primary-prevention patients, not a diagnostic test for an acute cardiac event.
To diagnose acute infarction
Acute infarction is diagnosed with serial troponin. High-sensitivity C-reactive protein is explicitly not for acute diagnosis.
To triage acute dyspnea
Dyspnea triage for suspected heart failure uses a natriuretic peptide.
To detect statin myopathy
Statin myopathy is evaluated with creatine kinase. Statins actually lower C-reactive protein.

A.io: Define: hemostasis, primary hemostasis, secondary hemostasis, thrombus, fibrinolysis, fibrin degradation products, D-dimer
A.q: A 44-year-old woman is taught the three overlapping stages of hemostasis. Which set is correct?
opts: Primary hemostasis, secondary hemostasis, fibrinolysis

Correct. Hemostasis has three overlapping stages: the platelet plug (primary hemostasis), the fibrin clot built by the coagulation factors (secondary hemostasis) and the breakdown of the clot (fibrinolysis).
Primary hemostasis, secondary hemostasis, thrombosis
Thrombosis is a pathologic clot forming in a vessel, not a stage of normal hemostasis. The third stage is fibrinolysis, the breakdown of the clot.
Platelet plug, fibrin clot, embolism
An embolism is a clot that has moved somewhere. The third stage of hemostasis is the dissolving of the clot by fibrinolysis.
Coagulation, thrombosis, embolism
These describe clot behavior in disease. Normal hemostasis runs from platelet plug, through coagulation, to fibrinolysis.

A.io: Discuss diagnostic testing for: primary hemostasis, secondary hemostasis, fibrinolysis
A.q: A 34-year-old man has hemarthroses and hematoma after surgery, with a normal prothrombin time, partial thromboplastin time and platelet count. Which next test fits?
opts: Factor VIII assay
A factor VIII assay addresses a prolonged partial thromboplastin time, which this patient does not have.
Euglobulin clot lysis time

Correct. This picture suggests deficiency of inhibitors of the fibrinolytic system, evaluated with euglobulin clot lysis time and testing for alpha-2 antiplasmin and plasminogen activator inhibitor 1.
A mixing study
A mixing study applies only when the prothrombin time or partial thromboplastin time is prolonged.
Platelet aggregation
Platelet disorders bring skin bruising, petechiae and mucosal bleeding, not hemarthroses and deep hematomas.

A.io: Measure and interpret the intervals, segments and waves of the cardiac cycle
A.q: What does the peak of the T wave mark?
opts: The end of ventricular depolarization
Ventricular depolarization ends with the QRS complex rather than at the peak of the T wave.
The start of atrial repolarization
Atrial repolarization is not represented as a distinct feature here.
The beginning of the ST segment
The ST segment begins at the J point and ends at the onset of the T wave.
The dividing line between the absolute and the relative refractory period
Correct, which is what makes a stimulus landing near the T wave peak so consequential: the cell has just become excitable again.

A.io: Discuss indications, advantages, and limitations of echocardiography
A.q: In which position does a patient lie initially for transthoracic echocardiography?
opts: Supine and flat throughout
The patient starts in the left lateral decubitus position and is repositioned.
Left lateral decubitus
Correct. It brings the heart toward the chest wall, and the patient is moved through other positions to obtain the different views.
Prone
The prone position is not used. The patient starts in left lateral decubitus and is repositioned for other views.
Standing
The study is performed lying, starting in the left lateral decubitus position.
A.cite: Cardiac Imaging and Vascular Studies - Elwaya.pptx, Slide 24

A.io: Describe action potentials and impulse conduction through the cardiac conduction system
A.q: What is the intrinsic firing rate of the sinoatrial node, the main pacemaker of the heart?
opts: 40 to 60 beats per minute
That is the intrinsic rate of the atrioventricular node, the back-up pacemaker; the sinoatrial node fires faster, at 60 to 100 beats per minute.
20 to 40 beats per minute
That is the intrinsic rate of the Purkinje network, the third pacemaker; the sinoatrial node fires much faster, at 60 to 100 beats per minute.
60 to 100 beats per minute
Correct. This is the fastest intrinsic rate in the conduction system, which is why the sinoatrial node normally sets the pace and the slower pacemakers stay in reserve.
100 to 150 beats per minute
That is faster than any structure in the conduction system fires on its own; the sinoatrial node's intrinsic rate is 60 to 100 beats per minute.

A.io: Describe the fundamental principles of electrocardiography
A.q: Which physical limb electrode was added to the original three to give four limb electrodes?
opts: Right arm
The right arm electrode was one of the original three; the one added later is the right leg electrode.
Right leg
Correct. The right leg electrode was added to the original three (right arm, left arm, left leg). It serves as a ground, and the four physical limb electrodes give the six hexaxial leads.
Left arm
The left arm electrode was one of the original three limb electrodes; the one added later is the right leg electrode.
Left leg
The left leg electrode was already one of the original three limb electrodes; the one added later is the right leg electrode.

A.io: Compare and contrast cardiac biomarkers: Creatine kinase, Cardiac troponins, BNP, hs-CRP
A.q: A 72-year-old woman has worsening dyspnea and leg edema. What does a raised B-type natriuretic peptide in her blood reflect?
opts: Myocyte necrosis
Necrosis releases troponin, the contractile regulatory protein. The natriuretic peptides are secreted in response to stretch, not released by dying cells.
Systemic inflammation
Inflammation is what C-reactive protein reflects, an acute-phase reactant made by the liver.
Skeletal muscle breakdown
Skeletal muscle injury is the territory of creatine kinase, for example in rhabdomyolysis or statin myopathy.
Myocardial wall stretch

Correct. B-type natriuretic peptide is released by the ventricles with volume or pressure overload. It reflects stretch rather than injury, a different mechanism from troponin, so the two are complementary.

A.io: Interpret common coagulation studies including: PT, INR, aPTT, D-dimer
A.q: A 28-year-old man has an isolated prolonged partial thromboplastin time that corrects on mixing, with a low factor VIII and normal von Willebrand antigen and activity. Which diagnosis fits?
opts: von Willebrand disease
von Willebrand disease would show abnormal von Willebrand antigen and activity.
Lupus anticoagulant
Lupus anticoagulant is an inhibitor that fails to correct on mixing, and it does not lower factor VIII.
Hemophilia
Correct. A low factor VIII with normal von Willebrand antigen and activity is hemophilia, and with abnormal von Willebrand studies it would be von Willebrand disease.
Dysfibrinogenemia
Dysfibrinogenemia is a fibrinogen function problem evaluated through fibrinogen activity and antigen, not factor VIII.

A.io: Describe laboratory findings associated with platelet abnormalities
A.q: A 27-year-old man has a normal platelet count and a bleeding time of 18 minutes (reference 3 to 10). What does this suggest?
opts: Platelets are not working well
Correct. With a normal platelet count a prolonged bleeding time signals a platelet function problem, a primary hemostasis defect.
Coagulation factors are deficient
Factor deficiencies prolong the prothrombin time or partial thromboplastin time, not bleeding time as the primary finding.
Fibrinolysis is excessive
Excess fibrinolysis is assessed by other tests, such as euglobulin clot lysis time. Bleeding time reflects the platelet plug.
The platelet count is falsely high
The count is normal, and a falsely high count would not lengthen the bleeding time.

A.io: Describe action potentials and impulse conduction through the cardiac conduction system
A.q: Why is phase 2 called the plateau?
opts: All ion movement stops entirely
Ions continue to move; it is the balance between two currents that holds the voltage steady.
Sodium continues to enter at a constant rate
Sodium channels have closed by this point; the inward current here is calcium.
Calcium entering the cell is matched by potassium moving the other way
Correct, and the calcium entering during this balance is what actually produces contraction, so the flat part of the trace is the working part of the beat. So the voltage holds.
The cell has returned to its resting voltage and remains there
The plateau sits well above the resting voltage, which is reached again at the end of phase three.

A.io: Discuss the use of lipid testing for cardiovascular risk assessment
A.q: A 54-year-old's 10-year PREVENT (Predicting Risk of cardiovascular disease EVENTs) estimate is 4%, in the borderline tier of 3% to under 5%. Besides discussing the estimate, what does the framework add for her?
opts: Evaluating risk enhancers
Correct. At borderline risk the framework pairs the risk discussion with an evaluation of risk enhancers, such as an elevated lipoprotein(a) or triglycerides of 150 mg/dL or above.
Immediate cardiac catheterization
No invasive testing is prompted by a risk estimate; the framework works through discussion, enhancers and a calcium score.
Serial troponin measurement
Serial troponin is for suspected acute coronary syndrome, not risk stratification in an asymptomatic person.
Stopping all lipid testing
Borderline risk calls for more information, not less; lipid testing continues.

A.io: Discuss indications, advantages, and limitations of echocardiography
A.q: Why is an intravenous sedative given before a transesophageal echocardiogram?
opts: To slow the heart for clearer images
Slowing the heart for images is the role of medication before cardiac computed tomography; the sedative here relaxes the patient and prevents vomiting.
To numb the back of the throat
A local anesthetic applied to the back of the throat does the numbing; the intravenous sedative relaxes the patient and prevents vomiting.
To relax the patient and prevent vomiting
Correct. The sedative helps the patient relax and prevents vomiting while the probe is passed through the mouth and down the esophagus.
To prevent a reaction to contrast
The sedative is given to relax the patient and prevent vomiting while the probe is passed, not to prevent a reaction to contrast; transesophageal echocardiography does not use iodinated contrast.

A.io: Discuss indications, advantages, and limitations of coronary angiography
A.q: How are the catheters for electrophysiological testing introduced?
opts: Through arteries into the left ventricle
Electrophysiological catheters are placed through veins into the right heart; arterial access to the left side is used for left heart catheterization.
Down the esophagus on an endoscope
The esophageal route belongs to transesophageal echocardiography; electrophysiological catheters are passed through veins into the right atrium or ventricle.
Into each coronary artery through the aorta
Entering each coronary artery is how angiography is done; electrophysiological catheters go through veins into the right atrium or right ventricle.
Through veins into the right heart
Correct. Three or four catheters pass from the internal jugular, subclavian or common femoral vein into the right atrium or right ventricle.

A.io: Discuss indications for ordering a lipid profile
A.q: A 40-year-old with no risk factors is due a routine lipid profile and has eaten breakfast. Is the sample acceptable?
opts: Yes, nonfasting is acceptable for most

Correct. Nonfasting is acceptable for most people. Fasting is reserved for triglycerides of 400 mg/dL or above, triglyceride disorders, or a family history of premature disease or genetic dyslipidemia.
No, every lipid profile must be fasting
Fasting is no longer required for most patients; it is reserved for specific situations.
No, lipids can only be drawn at night
No time-of-day rule applies to the lipid profile; the question is only whether fasting is needed.
Yes, but only lipoprotein(a) is valid
Lipoprotein(a) needs no fasting, but the standard nonfasting profile is also acceptable for most.

A.io: Discuss diagnostic testing for: primary hemostasis, secondary hemostasis, fibrinolysis
A.q: A 45-year-old woman has a fibrinogen of 0.4 grams per liter (reference 2.0 to 4.0) before traumatic surgery. What is the concern?
opts: Coronary artery disease
That risk applies to a very high fibrinogen, above 7.0 grams per liter.
Hemorrhage after surgery
Correct. A fibrinogen below 0.5 grams per liter can result in hemorrhage after traumatic surgery; low fibrinogen means bleeding.
Deep vein thrombosis
A low fibrinogen leaves too little substrate for clotting, raising bleeding risk. High fibrinogen is the clot concern.
Platelet clumping
Platelet clumping falsely lowers the automated platelet count and is unrelated to the fibrinogen level.

A.io: Compare and contrast cardiac biomarkers: Creatine kinase, Cardiac troponins, BNP, hs-CRP
A.q: A 23-year-old is brought in after collapsing during a marathon, with dark urine and painful thighs. Which marker best evaluates the suspected problem?
opts: Troponin I
Troponin I has cardiac specificity, which is the wrong target: the concern here is skeletal muscle, and creatine kinase is the test for that.
N-terminal pro B-type natriuretic peptide
The natriuretic peptides reflect cardiac wall stretch and are used for heart failure triage, not for muscle breakdown.
Lactate dehydrogenase
Lactate dehydrogenase is listed among markers no longer used to evaluate cardiac disease, and it is not the test for rhabdomyolysis.
Creatine kinase
Correct. Rhabdomyolysis is skeletal muscle injury, which is exactly where creatine kinase is still used. Its low cardiac specificity is no drawback here.

A.io: Analyze a lipid profile
A.q: A 58-year-old with diabetes has an LDL-C (low-density lipoprotein cholesterol) already below 70 mg/dL on therapy. Which test helps find remaining risk?
opts: HDL-C (high-density lipoprotein cholesterol)
Low HDL-C is a marker, not a therapeutic target, and it does not count atherogenic particles.
Creatine kinase
Creatine kinase evaluates skeletal muscle injury such as statin myopathy, not residual atherosclerotic risk.
ApoB (apolipoprotein B)
Correct. ApoB is used when triglycerides are 150 mg/dL or above, in diabetes, or when LDL-C is below 70 mg/dL, to find residual risk carried by atherogenic particles.
Troponin
Troponin is an acute myocardial injury marker, not a lipid risk marker.

A.io: Measure and interpret the intervals, segments and waves of the cardiac cycle
A.q: Why is the TP segment the best place to assess the isoelectric line?
opts: It is the longest segment on the tracing
Length is not the reason; the absence of electrical activity is.
It contains the J point
The J point sits between the QRS complex and the ST segment.
It is unaffected by lead placement
All parts of the tracing depend on lead placement; the TP segment is chosen because the cells are at rest.
It represents the resting state of the cardiac cells, between one T wave and the next P wave
Correct. Nothing electrical is happening there, so it gives the truest baseline against which to judge elevation or depression elsewhere.

A.io: Compare and contrast cardiovascular imaging modalities
A.q: On a vascular ultrasound, how does tissue density relate to the image?
opts: The denser the structure the darker it appears
The relationship runs the other way: dense structures return more signal and appear lighter.
Density does not affect the image, only depth does
Both matter: depth sets position on the screen and density sets brightness.
The denser the structure the lighter it appears
Correct, and superficial structures sit nearer the top of the screen, which together let you orient any image without being told what it is. So air is black and bone is near white.
Only flowing blood produces any signal
Tissue of all kinds reflects sound; Doppler is what adds flow information.

A.io: Discuss indications, advantages, and limitations of stress testing
A.q: Which exercise modalities are used, and which is preferred among the cycles?
opts: Treadmill and cycle ergometer
Correct, and arm ergometry exists for patients who cannot use their legs, which keeps the test available to more people. With the stationary bicycle preferred.
Treadmill only
Cycle ergometry is described alongside the treadmill as one of the two common modalities.
Arm ergometry, as first choice
Arm ergometry is listed but the stationary bicycle is the preferred cycle.
Step testing
Step testing is not among the modalities described, which are the treadmill, the cycle ergometer and arm ergometry.

A.io: Compare and contrast cardiac biomarkers: Creatine kinase, Cardiac troponins, BNP, hs-CRP
A.q: A 62-year-old has a troponin above the 99th percentile limit. What else must be present to call it a myocardial infarction?
opts: A raised creatine kinase as confirmation
Creatine kinase adds no diagnostic value for infarction once troponin is available, so it is not the confirming criterion.
Ischemia and a rising or falling pattern
Correct. Any troponin elevation is myocardial injury; infarction is injury plus ischemia plus a rising or falling pattern. Keeping the two apart is essential.
A raised B-type natriuretic peptide
B-type natriuretic peptide reflects stretch, not injury; it does not convert an injury into an infarction.
A value at least 10 times the limit
Ten times the limit is the threshold for bypass-related type 5 infarction, not the general definition.

A.io: Interpret common coagulation studies including: PT, INR, aPTT, D-dimer
A.q: A 26-year-old man has large palpable ecchymoses and bleeding into joints and muscles with hematoma formation. Which category fits?
opts: Platelet disorder
Platelet disorders typically cause skin bruising, petechiae and mucous membrane bleeding.
Clotting factor deficiency
Correct. Large palpable ecchymoses and bleeding into deep soft tissues, joints and muscles with hematoma are typical of a clotting factor deficiency.
Mild von Willebrand disease
Mild von Willebrand disease behaves like a platelet disorder, with mucosal and skin bleeding.
Spurious thrombocytopenia
Spurious thrombocytopenia is a counting artifact and causes no bleeding.

A.io: Discuss indications, advantages, and limitations of stress testing
A.q: A patient stops an exercise stress test having reached 70 percent of their predicted maximum heart rate, with no electrocardiographic changes. How should the result be read?
opts: Inadequate to exclude ischemia
Correct. The threshold for a valid test is 85 percent, so a negative result below it says nothing about the heart, only about the test.
A negative test, excluding ischemia
A negative result only counts once the heart rate threshold has been reached.
A positive test
Nothing here indicates ischemia; the problem is that the test was not taken far enough to say.
Equivocal, requiring repeat in six months
The result is uninterpretable rather than equivocal, and the stated consequence is that ischemia has not been excluded.

A.io: Interpret common coagulation studies including: PT, INR, aPTT, D-dimer
A.q: A 35-year-old woman has a prothrombin time of 19 seconds (reference 11 to 13) and a normal activated partial thromboplastin time. Which deficiency fits?
opts: Factor VII
Correct. An isolated prolonged prothrombin time points to the extrinsic pathway, factor VII deficiency.
Factor VIII
Factor VIII deficiency prolongs the activated partial thromboplastin time and leaves the prothrombin time normal.
Factor IX
Factor IX deficiency, hemophilia B, prolongs the activated partial thromboplastin time with a normal prothrombin time.
Factor XI
Factor XI deficiency prolongs the activated partial thromboplastin time and spares the prothrombin time.

B.io: Discuss indications, advantages, and limitations of echocardiography
B.q: What distinguishes a transthoracic from a transesophageal echocardiogram?
opts: One uses Doppler and the other does not
Both can use Doppler. What separates them is whether the transducer sits outside the body or inside it.
One uses ionizing radiation while the other does not
Neither uses ionizing radiation. The difference is the position of the transducer, outside the body or within it.
The transducer is outside the body in one, inside in the other
Correct, and everything else about the two -- invasiveness, sedation, contraindications, and how much posterior detail you get -- follows from that single difference.
One assesses valves and the other assesses chambers
Both assess valves and chambers; the difference is the transducer position.

B.io: Identify the standard limb and precordial leads and their proper anatomical placement
B.q: Which of these is one of the described contiguous groups?
opts: Leads I, II and III
These three are the bipolar limb leads rather than a contiguous group.
Leads II, III and aVF
Correct. The other two groups are V1 to V4, and leads I, aVL, V5 and V6.
Leads aVR, aVL and aVF
These are the augmented leads rather than a contiguous group.
Leads V1, V3 and V5
The described group runs V1 to V4 consecutively rather than alternating.

B.io: Describe laboratory findings associated with platelet abnormalities
B.q: A 61-year-old man has a platelet count of 6,000 per microliter (adult reference 140,000 to 400,000). Which risk is highest?
opts: Spontaneous intracranial bleeding
Correct. Below 10,000 per microliter the patient is at risk for spontaneous intracranial bleeding and serious hemorrhage.
Bruising only with major trauma
Bruising easily starts below 50,000 per microliter. At 6,000 the risk is far greater than bruising with major trauma.
Excess bleeding only with surgery
At this count bleeding is spontaneous, and surgery is not needed to provoke it.
No added risk until the count is lower still
Below 10,000 per microliter is already the highest-risk tier, with risk of spontaneous intracranial bleeding.

B.io: Describe the fundamental principles of electrocardiography
B.q: A strip has no three-second markers. How many large boxes make up a six-second strip?
opts: Thirty large boxes
Correct. Each large box is 0.2 seconds, so fifteen large boxes make 3 seconds and thirty make 6 seconds.
Fifteen large boxes
Fifteen large boxes at 0.2 seconds each is only 3 seconds; a six-second strip needs thirty large boxes.
Five large boxes
Five large boxes is just one second, since each is 0.2 seconds; a six-second strip needs thirty large boxes.
Sixty large boxes
Sixty large boxes at 0.2 seconds each would be 12 seconds; a six-second strip needs thirty large boxes.

B.io: Interpret common coagulation studies including: PT, INR, aPTT, D-dimer
B.q: A 27-year-old woman has a low platelet count with a normal prothrombin time, partial thromboplastin time and platelet function analysis. Which diagnosis fits?
opts: Immune thrombocytopenia
Correct. Immune thrombocytopenia, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, hemolytic uremic syndrome and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia all give a low count with normal clotting times.
Disseminated intravascular coagulation
Disseminated intravascular coagulation also has a low count but prolongs the prothrombin time and partial thromboplastin time.
von Willebrand disease
von Willebrand disease has a normal platelet count and a prolonged partial thromboplastin time.
Early liver failure
Early liver failure prolongs the prothrombin time and leaves the platelet count normal.

B.io: Discuss indications for ordering a lipid profile
B.q: A 41-year-old man is found to have a markedly elevated lipoprotein(a) after a premature myocardial infarction. Whom should testing be extended to?
opts: No one; it is not inherited
It is more than 90% genetically determined, which is exactly why family testing makes sense.
Only his spouse
A spouse shares no genes with him. Cascade testing moves through blood relatives.
His first-degree relatives

Correct. Testing is indicated in those with a personal or family history of atherosclerotic disease, with cascade testing in appropriate families, because the level is more than 90% genetically determined.
Only relatives over 65
Nothing restricts cascade testing by age; the level is stable over life and can be measured at any adult age.

B.io: Discuss indications, advantages, and limitations of stress testing
B.q: Which of these is a stated indication for exercise stress testing?
opts: Cardiac assessment before non-cardiac surgery in a high-risk patient
Correct, alongside symptoms suggesting ischemia, known ischemic disease with a change in status, prior revascularization and newly diagnosed heart failure.
Acute chest pain before acute coronary syndrome has been excluded
The indication applies specifically after acute coronary syndrome and infarction have been excluded, not before.
Suspected aortic dissection
Dissection is assessed by imaging the aorta rather than by stressing the heart.
Screening an asymptomatic patient with no risk factors
Screening in that setting is not among the listed indications.

B.io: Determine heart rate using an electrocardiogram
B.q: A six-second strip contains eight QRS complexes. What is the ventricular rate?
opts: Forty-eight beats per minute
That would follow from multiplying by six rather than by ten.
Eighty beats per minute
Correct. The six-second method multiplies the count by ten, since six seconds is a tenth of a minute.
Eight beats per minute
That is the raw count over six seconds rather than the rate per minute.
One hundred and sixty beats per minute
That would follow from doubling the correct figure; the six-second count is multiplied by ten.

B.io: Describe the fundamental principles of electrocardiography
B.q: In which direction does conduction truly travel through the heart?
opts: Right and up, toward the shoulder
The described pathway runs leftward and downward rather than to the right and upward.
Left and down, toward the anterior chest
Correct, and this is why lead II sees the beat so well: it looks along that axis.
Straight downward, in the coronal plane only
The described direction has a leftward and anterior component as well as a downward one.
Posteriorly, away from the chest wall
It runs left and down toward the anterior chest rather than posteriorly away from it.

B.io: Discuss indications for ordering cardiac biomarkers
B.q: A 71-year-old has troponin monitored after coronary artery bypass grafting. Which rise defines a surgery-related (type 5) infarction?
opts: More than 5 times the 99th percentile limit
More than 5 times the limit defines type 4a, the infarction related to percutaneous coronary intervention.
Any value above the 99th percentile limit
At least one value above the limit is the type 4b criterion, not the bypass-related definition.
More than 2 times the 99th percentile limit
No infarction type is defined at twice the limit. The procedural thresholds are 5 times for percutaneous intervention and 10 times for bypass surgery.
More than 10 times the 99th percentile limit
Correct. Coronary artery bypass graft-related infarction, type 5, needs more than 10 times the 99th percentile upper reference limit, a higher bar than for percutaneous intervention.

B.io: Compare and contrast cardiovascular imaging modalities
B.q: How does a vascular ultrasound image form?
opts: Ionizing radiation is absorbed differently by tissues of differing density
That describes radiography; ultrasound uses no ionizing radiation.
Quartz crystals emit pulses that reflect off tissue

Correct. The returning echoes are what the machine turns into a picture, so anything that stops sound returning leaves a gap in it. The pulses are high frequency, and what returns depends on the density of what they meet.
A magnetic field aligns protons which then emit radiofrequency signal
That describes magnetic resonance. Ultrasound works by emitting sound pulses and reading the returning echoes.
An injected tracer is taken up and emits gamma rays
That describes nuclear imaging. Ultrasound forms its image from reflected high-frequency sound.

B.io: Compare and contrast cardiac biomarkers: Creatine kinase, Cardiac troponins, BNP, hs-CRP
B.q: A 64-year-old woman has ischemic chest pain. Which troponin result supports acute myocardial infarction?
opts: A value above the 50th percentile of healthy adults
The median of a healthy population is not the threshold. The limit is set so that only 1 in 100 healthy people would exceed it.
Any detectable troponin at all on a sensitive assay
High-sensitivity assays can measure troponin in healthy people, so mere detectability is not the criterion. The value must exceed the 99th percentile limit.
A value above the 99th percentile upper reference limit

Correct. Under the Fourth Universal Definition, infarction is evidence of myocardial injury, troponin I or T above the 99th percentile upper reference limit, in the appropriate setting of ischemic symptoms.
A value above the 95th percentile of hospital patients
The reference population is healthy people, not hospital patients, and the percentile is the 99th, not the 95th.

B.io: Describe the fundamental principles of electrocardiography
B.q: In most leads, how far from the baseline may a normal J point sit?
opts: Within 3 millimeters
That allows far too much variance for most leads; the J point should be at the baseline with only 1 millimeter of variance.
Within 5 millimeters, one large box
That is a whole large box of displacement; the J point should sit at the baseline with only 1 millimeter of variance.
Within 1 millimeter
Correct. The J point, where the QRS complex ends and the ST segment begins, should be at the baseline, with one millimeter of variance allowed.
Exactly on the baseline, with no allowance
That is stricter than the rule; the J point should be at the baseline but 1 millimeter of variance is allowed.

B.io: Interpret common coagulation studies including: PT, INR, aPTT, D-dimer
B.q: A 47-year-old woman has a prolonged partial thromboplastin time that does not correct on mixing, and the abnormality depends on phospholipid. Which diagnosis fits?
opts: A specific factor inhibitor
A specific factor inhibitor fails to correct but is not phospholipid dependent.
Hemophilia A
Hemophilia A corrects on mixing and does not show phospholipid-dependent inhibition.
Lupus anticoagulant
Correct. Failure to correct with phospholipid dependence, shown by the dilute Russell viper venom time, is lupus anticoagulant.
Hypofibrinogenemia
Hypofibrinogenemia is diagnosed by low fibrinogen activity and low antigen, not by phospholipid dependence.

B.io: Discuss diagnostic testing for: primary hemostasis, secondary hemostasis, fibrinolysis
B.q: A 12-year-old boy has a prolonged partial thromboplastin time that corrects when mixed one to one with normal plasma. What does this suggest?
opts: An inhibitor
An inhibitor also blocks the factors in the normal plasma, so the prolonged time persists after mixing.
Lupus anticoagulant
Lupus anticoagulant is an inhibitor, so the prolonged time does not correct with normal plasma.
A factor deficiency
Correct. Correction on a mixing study suggests a factor deficiency, because normal plasma supplies the missing factor.
A platelet disorder
Platelet disorders give a normal partial thromboplastin time, so a mixing study is not used for them.

B.io: Discuss diagnostic testing for: primary hemostasis, secondary hemostasis, fibrinolysis
B.q: A 26-year-old woman has a bedside bleeding time after a standardized forearm puncture. What is being timed?
opts: How long plasma takes to clot with tissue factor
That describes the prothrombin time, a laboratory test of the extrinsic pathway on plasma in a tube.
How long plasma takes to clot with a phospholipid activator
That describes the activated partial thromboplastin time, which assesses the intrinsic pathway in a laboratory tube.
How long the puncture keeps bleeding
Correct. Bleeding time is the time in minutes for a standardized, superficial skin puncture to stop bleeding, and it is performed at the bedside.
How long a formed clot takes to dissolve
Clot dissolution is fibrinolysis, studied by tests such as D-dimer. Bleeding time measures how long a skin puncture bleeds.

B.io: Discuss indications, advantages, and limitations of coronary angiography
B.q: Which complications of coronary angiography occur at the catheter insertion site?
opts: Contrast nephropathy and arrhythmia
Both are recognized risks of the procedure but are not site complications.
Hematoma and pseudoaneurysm
Correct, and the pseudoaneurysm is the one to check for deliberately, since it maintains a continuous communication with the artery.
Esophageal perforation
That belongs to transesophageal echocardiography rather than to arterial catheterization.
Pneumothorax
Not among the described site complications, which are hematoma and pseudoaneurysm.

B.io: Discuss indications for ordering cardiac biomarkers
B.q: A 54-year-old man started a statin two months ago and now has diffuse muscle aches. Which biomarker is the appropriate test?
opts: Creatine kinase
Correct. Statin myopathy and rhabdomyolysis are skeletal muscle questions, and creatine kinase is the right test for them. Troponin is not.
High-sensitivity troponin
Troponin answers whether cardiac myocytes are injured. For suspected skeletal muscle injury from a statin, creatine kinase is the appropriate test.
B-type natriuretic peptide
B-type natriuretic peptide reflects ventricular wall stretch and is ordered for suspected heart failure, not for muscle symptoms.
High-sensitivity C-reactive protein
It is an inflammatory risk marker for atherosclerotic disease. Statins actually lower it, but it does not evaluate muscle injury.

B.io: Discuss indications, advantages, and limitations of nuclear cardiology studies
B.q: Tracer uptake in a region is normal at rest but reduced after stress. What does that pattern indicate?
opts: Inducible ischemia, from a coronary stenosis
Correct. The tissue is alive but cannot increase its supply when demand rises, which is what a stenosis does.
Infarcted, non-viable tissue
Infarcted tissue shows no uptake in either set. Reduced uptake only after stress indicates inducible ischemia.
Normal myocardium
Normal tissue maintains or increases uptake under stress rather than losing it.
A pericardial effusion
Pericardial fluid is not assessed by perfusion imaging; the pattern described indicates inducible ischemia.

B.io: Analyze a lipid profile
B.q: A 49-year-old has triglycerides of 180 mg/dL (desirable below 150 mg/dL) and no other lipid abnormality. How is this triglyceride level classed?
opts: A risk enhancer for atherosclerotic disease
Correct. Triglycerides of 150 mg/dL or above mean increased atherosclerotic risk and act as a risk enhancer; severe hypertriglyceridemia begins at 500 mg/dL.
Severe hypertriglyceridemia
Severe hypertriglyceridemia starts at 500 mg/dL, with pancreatitis risk; this level is well below that.
Normal, with no significance
It is above the desirable limit, so it is not insignificant; it raises atherosclerotic risk.
Diagnostic of familial hypercholesterolemia
Familial hypercholesterolemia is a cholesterol disorder flagged by very high LDL-C (low-density lipoprotein cholesterol), not by a modest triglyceride rise.

B.io: Discuss the use of lipid testing for cardiovascular risk assessment
B.q: A 37-year-old with no symptoms asks whether she needs a lipoprotein(a) level. What does the current guidance say?
opts: Measure it only after a heart attack
Testing is not limited to people with established disease; all adults are measured at least once.
Measure it at least once in all adults
Correct. Current multisociety guidance recommends measuring lipoprotein(a) at least once in all adults for atherosclerotic risk assessment.
Measure it every year from age 40
It is stable and largely genetic, so a single lifetime measurement generally suffices.
Never measure it; it is untreatable
Its value lies in risk assessment, and elevation prompts more intensive management of other risk factors.

B.io: Measure and interpret the intervals, segments and waves of the cardiac cycle
B.q: What does the R wave represent?
opts: Depolarization of the anterior left ventricle
Correct, and it is the first positive deflection, following either the PR interval or the Q wave.
Depolarization of the interventricular septum
That is the Q wave, the first negative deflection following the PR interval.
Depolarization of the lateral wall of the left ventricle
That is the S wave, the first negative deflection following the R wave.
Depolarization of the atria
Atrial depolarization is the P wave rather than any component of the QRS complex.

B.io: Describe the fundamental principles of electrocardiography
B.q: What is the normal corrected QT interval range in a man?
opts: 360 to 460 milliseconds
That is the normal corrected QT range for a woman; in a man it is 350 to 450 milliseconds.
450 to 500 milliseconds
That band is borderline or prolonged for a corrected QT, not normal; the normal QT interval in a man is 350 to 450 milliseconds.
400 to 500 milliseconds
That reaches into the prolonged range, up to the 500 millisecond threshold; the normal QT interval in a man is 350 to 450 milliseconds.
350 to 450 milliseconds
Correct. The corrected QT interval, which adjusts for heart rate, is normally 350 to 450 milliseconds in men; the female range is slightly higher, at 360 to 460 milliseconds.

B.io: Discuss the use of lipid testing for cardiovascular risk assessment
B.q: A 58-year-old's 10-year PREVENT (Predicting Risk of cardiovascular disease EVENTs) estimate is 7%, in the intermediate tier of 5% to under 10%, and she is unsure about starting therapy. What may be considered to reclassify her risk?
opts: A high-sensitivity troponin
Troponin addresses acute injury, not long-term risk reclassification.
A B-type natriuretic peptide
The natriuretic peptides are for heart failure; they are not the reclassification tool in this framework.
A coronary artery calcium score

Correct. In the Calculate, Personalize, Reclassify framework, when there is clinical or patient uncertainty at borderline or intermediate risk, a coronary artery calcium score is considered to revise the estimate.
A creatine kinase
Creatine kinase evaluates muscle injury and has no role in cardiovascular risk reclassification.

B.io: Discuss indications, advantages, and limitations of echocardiography
B.q: Which history contraindicates a transesophageal echocardiogram?
opts: Cerebral ischemia
Cerebral ischemia is an indication, because the study can find left atrial appendage thrombus as the source, rather than a contraindication.
A prosthetic heart valve
Assessing a prosthetic valve and its current function is an indication for the transesophageal study, not a reason to avoid it.
Odynophagia or dysphagia
Correct. A history of painful or difficult swallowing is a contraindication, since a probe must be passed down the esophagus and swallowed to advance.
Aortic dilation
Aortic dilation, dissection and arteritis are indications for the transesophageal study, which shows the aorta in more detail than a chest wall view.
