These are right heart measurements. The left heart study assesses coronary anatomy and the systemic side.
Coronary anatomy, aortic pressure and left ventricular function

Correct. Everything on the systemic side of the circulation, which is the side the left heart serves. Together with systemic vascular resistance, and aortic and mitral valve function, and left ventricular pressure.
Tricuspid and pulmonic valve function
These are assessed at right heart catheterization; the left study covers the aortic and mitral valves.
Right atrial pressure
That is a right heart measurement rather than one obtained from the left side.
D.cite: Cardiac Imaging and Vascular Studies - Elwaya.pptx, Slide 68

D.io: Describe laboratory findings associated with platelet abnormalities
D.q: A 65-year-old man with uremia bleeds easily. His platelet count, prothrombin time and partial thromboplastin time are normal. Which category fits?
opts: Factor VII deficiency
Factor VII deficiency prolongs the prothrombin time, which is normal here.
Platelet dysfunction
Correct. Normal prothrombin time and partial thromboplastin time with bleeding suggest platelet dysfunction; uremia is one cause, and platelet function testing is abnormal.
Hemophilia A
Hemophilia A prolongs the partial thromboplastin time, which is normal here.
Hypofibrinogenemia
Low fibrinogen prolongs the prothrombin time and partial thromboplastin time, and both are normal here.

D.io: Describe action potentials and impulse conduction through the cardiac conduction system
D.q: Which fascicle of the left bundle branch extends across the anterior wall of the left ventricle?
opts: The left posterior fascicle
The left posterior fascicle extends across the posterior aspect of the left ventricle rather than the anterior wall.
The left anterior fascicle
Correct. Of the left fascicles it is the one that extends across the anterior wall of the left ventricle.
The intraventricular septal fascicle
The septal fascicle extends across the interventricular septum; it is the left anterior fascicle that crosses the anterior wall.
The right bundle branch
The right bundle branch is not a fascicle of the left bundle branch; it supplies the right ventricle.

D.io: Measure and interpret the intervals, segments and waves of the cardiac cycle
D.q: Where is the U wave best seen, and what is it thought to represent?
opts: In lead II, representing atrial repolarization
It is best seen in the anterior precordial leads, and atrial repolarization is not the proposed explanation.
In aVR, representing septal depolarization
Septal depolarization is the Q wave, and the U wave is best seen in V2 and V3.
In V2 and V3, possibly repolarization of the Purkinje fibers
Correct, and the hedging is honest: there is no clear understanding of what it represents, so the association with electrolytes is more useful than the theory.
In V5 and V6, representing delayed ventricular filling
The leads are V2 and V3, and the proposal concerns Purkinje repolarization.

D.io: Discuss indications, advantages, and limitations of echocardiography
D.q: What does Doppler add to an echocardiogram?
opts: Myocardial tracer uptake
Tracer uptake is what nuclear perfusion imaging measures with a gamma camera; Doppler uses sound to measure flow and velocity, not a tracer.
The coronary calcium burden
Calcium scoring is a non-contrast cardiac computed tomography measurement; Doppler adds blood flow and velocity to the echocardiogram instead.
Blood flow and velocity
Correct. Doppler shows flow and velocity through the heart chambers and great vessels, which the grayscale picture of structure alone does not provide.
Electrical conduction pathways
Conduction is investigated by electrophysiological testing; Doppler adds information about blood flow and its velocity through the heart.
D.cite: Cardiac Imaging and Vascular Studies - Elwaya.pptx, Slide 20

D.io: Define: hemostasis, primary hemostasis, secondary hemostasis, thrombus, fibrinolysis, fibrin degradation products, D-dimer
D.q: A 22-year-old woman has von Willebrand disease. Which phase of hemostasis does the missing factor serve?
opts: Secondary hemostasis
Secondary hemostasis is the coagulation cascade that makes cross-linked fibrin. von Willebrand factor acts earlier, at the platelet plug.
Fibrinolysis
Fibrinolysis is the plasmin-mediated breakdown of a clot. von Willebrand factor helps platelets stick, which comes first.
Primary hemostasis
Correct. von Willebrand factor tethers platelets to exposed subendothelial collagen, so its deficiency impairs formation of the platelet plug.
Vasoconstriction
Vasoconstriction narrows the injured vessel and is a separate component of hemostasis. von Willebrand factor tethers platelets to collagen.

D.io: Compare and contrast lipids and lipoproteins involved in atherosclerotic disease
D.q: A 49-year-old asks which lipoprotein is the principal driver of atherosclerotic disease. Which is it?
opts: HDL (high-density lipoprotein)
HDL performs reverse cholesterol transport, a protective role that contrasts with the apoB particles.
Chylomicrons
Chylomicrons carry dietary triglyceride; their remnants are atherogenic, but LDL is the principal driver.
Albumin
Albumin is not a lipoprotein and plays no role in the atherogenic particle list.
LDL (low-density lipoprotein)
Correct. LDL is the major cholesterol carrier and the primary target for prevention; LDL cholesterol and cardiovascular risk have a log-linear relationship.

D.io: Discuss indications, advantages, and limitations of stress testing
D.q: For which patient is an echocardiographic stress test the appropriate initial choice?
opts: One who cannot exercise at all
A patient unable to exercise is given a pharmacological stress test.
One with a normal resting electrocardiogram who can exercise
That patient can have the standard exercise test, which is simpler.
One with suspected aortic dissection
Dissection is assessed by imaging the aorta rather than by stress testing.
One who can exercise but whose resting tracing is abnormal
Correct. The electrocardiogram cannot be read for ischemia if it is already abnormal, so the imaging has to carry the answer instead.
D.cite: Cardiac Imaging and Vascular Studies - Elwaya.pptx, Slide 37

D.io: Compare and contrast cardiac biomarkers: Creatine kinase, Cardiac troponins, BNP, hs-CRP
D.q: A 74-year-old has an N-terminal pro B-type natriuretic peptide drawn. Where does this molecule come from?
opts: It is the inert fragment of cleaved pro-BNP
Correct. Cardiomyocytes secrete pro B-type natriuretic peptide in response to stretch, and it is cleaved into biologically active BNP (B-type natriuretic peptide) and inert NT-proBNP.
It is the active hormone made by the liver
The liver makes C-reactive protein. The natriuretic peptides come from cardiomyocytes, and the N-terminal fragment is the inert one.
It is released when myocytes become necrotic
Necrosis releases troponin. The natriuretic peptides are secreted in response to stretch, as in rising pressure from heart failure.
It is a troponin subunit found in the atria
The troponin subunits are T, I and C. NT-proBNP (N-terminal pro B-type natriuretic peptide) is a natriuretic peptide fragment.

D.io: Discuss indications for ordering cardiac biomarkers
D.q: A 58-year-old still has an elevated troponin four weeks after a myocardial infarction. What does a late elevation relate to?
opts: Higher left ventricular ejection fraction
The relationship is inverse: the higher the late troponin, the lower the ejection fraction.
A falsely positive assay
A late elevation after a known infarction carries meaning about its size and impact rather than being an assay error.
Lower left ventricular ejection fraction
Correct. Elevated late levels at 4 weeks are inversely related to left ventricular ejection fraction, which is how troponin estimates infarct size and impact.
A reduced risk of reinfarction
The late value relates to infarct size and ventricular function, not to protection against reinfarction.

D.io: Discuss indications for ordering cardiac biomarkers
D.q: A 65-year-old had a stent placed yesterday and his chest pain has returned. Which use of troponin applies?
opts: Guiding heart failure therapy
Guiding heart failure therapy is an application of the natriuretic peptides, not of troponin.
Screening for statin myopathy
Statin myopathy is evaluated with creatine kinase. Troponin is aimed at cardiac myocyte injury.
Refining long-term risk
Long-term risk refinement is the role of high-sensitivity C-reactive protein and the lipid profile.
Detecting reinfarction
Correct. Troponins detect reocclusion and reinfarction, and procedure-related infarction, among their applications beyond the first diagnosis.

D.io: Discuss diagnostic testing for: primary hemostasis, secondary hemostasis, fibrinolysis
D.q: A 5-year-old girl has lifelong severe bleeding of any tissue, and all screening clotting tests are normal. Which specific assay is next?
opts: Factor VIII assay
A factor VIII assay is for a prolonged partial thromboplastin time.
Factor XIII assay
Correct. When screens are normal and factor XIII deficiency is suspected, the next tests are a clot stability test and a factor XIII assay.
Mixing study
A mixing study is for a prolonged clotting time and is not needed when the screens are normal.
Fibrinogen antigen
Fibrinogen antigen follows a low fibrinogen activity, which is not the case here.

D.io: Discuss indications, advantages, and limitations of cardiac MRI
D.q: What is done before a cardiovascular magnetic resonance study is ordered?
opts: An echocardiogram
Correct. It is the first-line functional study, and magnetic resonance answers what it leaves unresolved rather than replacing it.
A coronary angiogram
Angiography is invasive and is not a prerequisite for magnetic resonance.
A nuclear perfusion study
A perfusion study is not the stated prerequisite; an echocardiogram is done before magnetic resonance is ordered.
A coronary calcium score
Calcium scoring is not the stated prerequisite; an echocardiogram is done first.
D.cite: Cardiac Imaging and Vascular Studies - Elwaya.pptx, Slide 56

D.io: Identify common abnormal cardiovascular imaging findings
D.q: In which patients is cephalization seen?
opts: Pneumothorax and pleural effusion
Neither is given as a cause. Cephalization is seen in heart failure and pulmonary hypertension.
Coronary artery disease without failure
Coronary disease alone does not produce it; the sign follows raised pulmonary pressure in failure or pulmonary hypertension.
Heart failure and pulmonary hypertension
Correct. Both raise pressure in the pulmonary circulation, and the redistribution upward is the radiographic consequence.
Pericardial calcification
Calcification is listed as a separate radiographic finding rather than as a form of cephalization.
D.cite: Cardiac Imaging and Vascular Studies - Elwaya.pptx, Slide 9

D.io: Interpret common coagulation studies including: PT, INR, aPTT, D-dimer
D.q: A 62-year-old woman has normal prothrombin time, partial thromboplastin time, fibrinogen and platelets, and a raised D-dimer. Which interpretation fits?
opts: Disseminated intravascular coagulation
Disseminated intravascular coagulation would also prolong the clotting times and lower fibrinogen and platelets.
Hemophilia A
Hemophilia A prolongs the partial thromboplastin time, which is normal here.
Platelet dysfunction
Platelet dysfunction does not raise D-dimer and is not reflected by the coagulation screens.
Acute thrombosis
Correct. A raised D-dimer with normal coagulation studies and platelets is the acute thrombosis pattern, and D-dimer is nonspecific.

D.io: Interpret common coagulation studies including: PT, INR, aPTT, D-dimer
D.q: A 15-year-old boy has a prolonged prothrombin time and partial thromboplastin time with a normal thrombin time. Which deficiency fits?
opts: Factor X, V or II
Correct. A prolonged prothrombin time and partial thromboplastin time with a normal thrombin time points to deficiency of common pathway factors, factor X, V or II.
Factor VII only
Factor VII deficiency prolongs only the prothrombin time, not the partial thromboplastin time.
Factor VIII only
Factor VIII deficiency prolongs only the partial thromboplastin time.
Hypofibrinogenemia
Hypofibrinogenemia would prolong the thrombin time, which is normal here.

D.io: Discuss indications, advantages, and limitations of echocardiography
D.q: Why is transthoracic echocardiography the most common echo procedure?
opts: It can be performed at the bedside and is noninvasive
Correct. Availability rather than image quality is what makes it the default, and the trade is detail at the back of the heart.
It gives better detail of the posterior structures
Posterior and inferior detail is exactly where it is weaker than the transesophageal study.
It requires no operator training
Operator dependence applies to ultrasound generally. Its advantage is being noninvasive and available at the bedside.
It is the only echo that can use Doppler
Doppler is available in both studies. The transthoracic study leads because it is noninvasive and bedside-capable.
D.cite: Cardiac Imaging and Vascular Studies - Elwaya.pptx, Slide 22

D.io: Interpret common coagulation studies including: PT, INR, aPTT, D-dimer
D.q: A 50-year-old woman with sepsis is evaluated for disseminated intravascular coagulation. Which finding is decreased?
opts: Fibrin degradation products
Fibrin degradation products are elevated in this condition, because clots are being broken down.
Prothrombin time
The prothrombin time is prolonged in this condition, not decreased, because factors are consumed.
Activated partial thromboplastin time
The partial thromboplastin time is prolonged, not decreased.
Protein C, antithrombin and protein S
Correct. In disseminated intravascular coagulation the protease inhibitors, including protein C, antithrombin and protein S, are decreased.

D.io: Define: hemostasis, primary hemostasis, secondary hemostasis, thrombus, fibrinolysis, fibrin degradation products, D-dimer
D.q: A 60-year-old woman has a vessel injury, and a physician explains how the clot is stabilized. Which phase forms insoluble, cross-linked fibrin through thrombin?
opts: Primary hemostasis
Primary hemostasis builds the platelet plug with von Willebrand factor and platelet aggregation. Fibrin is not formed until the coagulation factors act.
Fibrinolysis
Fibrinolysis dissolves fibrin; plasmin degrades it. It removes the clot rather than forming the fibrin mesh.
Secondary hemostasis
Correct. Secondary hemostasis is formation of insoluble, cross-linked fibrin by activated coagulation factors, specifically thrombin; the coagulation cascade drives it.
Vasoconstriction
Vasoconstriction narrows the injured vessel and is one of the three classic components of hemostasis, but it does not form fibrin.

D.io: Discuss indications, advantages, and limitations of coronary angiography
D.q: What is coronary angiography the gold standard for?
opts: Assessing myocardial viability
Viability is assessed by nuclear perfusion imaging or magnetic resonance.
Coronary artery anatomy and cardiac function
Correct, which is why it is usually performed before any percutaneous or surgical intervention on the coronary arteries.
Measuring the coronary calcium score
Calcium scoring is a non-contrast computed tomography study.
Detecting valve vegetations
Vegetations are sought on echocardiography. Angiography is the gold standard for coronary anatomy and cardiac function.
D.cite: Cardiac Imaging and Vascular Studies - Elwaya.pptx, Slide 66

D.io: Discuss the use of lipid testing for cardiovascular risk assessment
D.q: A 50-year-old has an elevated lipoprotein(a) and an LDL-C (low-density lipoprotein cholesterol) at goal on a statin. What does the elevated lipoprotein(a) prompt?
opts: Doubling the statin to lower the lipoprotein(a)
Statins do not lower lipoprotein(a); it is described as statin-resistant.
Earlier, more intensive control of other risk factors

Correct. Lipoprotein(a) is a largely fixed genetic risk factor measured once; elevation prompts earlier and more intensive management of every other modifiable risk factor, since statins do not lower it.
Repeating lipoprotein(a) every 3 months
It is stable and measured once, so frequent repetition would not change anything.
No change, since it is not a risk factor
It is highly atherogenic, per particle more so than LDL (low-density lipoprotein), and its elevation is a risk enhancer.

D.io: Interpret common coagulation studies including: PT, INR, aPTT, D-dimer
D.q: A 41-year-old man bleeds despite a normal platelet count, platelet function, prothrombin time and partial thromboplastin time. Which deficiency should be considered?
opts: Hemophilia A
Hemophilia A prolongs the partial thromboplastin time, which is normal in this patient.
Factor VII deficiency
Factor VII deficiency prolongs the prothrombin time, which is normal in this patient.
Factor XIII deficiency

Correct. Factor XIII or alpha-2 antiplasmin deficiency fits: normal prothrombin time and partial thromboplastin time with bleeding suggest a platelet disorder, mild von Willebrand disease, factor XIII or alpha-2 antiplasmin deficiency, or impaired fibrinolysis.
Heparin effect
Heparin prolongs the partial thromboplastin time and thrombin time.

D.io: Describe action potentials and impulse conduction through the cardiac conduction system
D.q: Into how many fascicles does the left bundle branch divide, and what are they?
opts: Two: the left anterior and the left posterior
A third, the interventricular septal fascicle, is described alongside these two.
Four, one to each wall of the ventricle
Three fascicles are described: the left posterior, the interventricular septal and the left anterior.
It does not divide; it terminates directly in Purkinje fibers
It divides into fascicles before becoming the Purkinje network.
Three: left anterior, left posterior and septal
Correct. The septal fascicle is the one most often forgotten, which matters because the three-fascicle arrangement is what makes bifascicular block possible. The left anterior.

D.io: Describe action potentials and impulse conduction through the cardiac conduction system
D.q: Where does the sinoatrial node sit?
opts: In the upper wall of the right atrium
Correct, and being the highest pacemaker in the chain is what makes it the one that normally sets the rate. Just below the opening of the vena cava.
At the junction of the atria and the ventricles
That is where the atrioventricular node sits, near the coronary sinus, rather than the sinoatrial node.
Within the interventricular septum
The septum carries the bundle of His and its branches rather than the sinoatrial node.
In the wall of the left atrium
It sits in the upper wall of the RIGHT atrium, just below the opening of the vena cava.

D.io: Compare and contrast lipids and lipoproteins involved in atherosclerotic disease
D.q: A 42-year-old eats a fatty meal and chylomicrons appear in her plasma. Which apolipoprotein do they carry?
opts: ApoB-100 (apolipoprotein B-100), made by the liver
ApoB-100 is the hepatic form found in VLDL (very low-density lipoprotein), IDL (intermediate-density lipoprotein), LDL (low-density lipoprotein) and lipoprotein(a).
ApoB-48 (apolipoprotein B-48), made by the intestine
Correct. ApoB-48 is synthesized by the intestines and found in chylomicrons, which carry dietary triglyceride.
ApoA-I (apolipoprotein A-I), made by the liver
ApoA-I is the major structural protein of HDL (high-density lipoprotein), not of chylomicrons.
Apo(a) (apolipoprotein(a)), made by the liver
Apo(a) bound to apoB-100 forms lipoprotein(a); it is not a chylomicron protein.

D.io: Compare and contrast lipids and lipoproteins involved in atherosclerotic disease
D.q: A 44-year-old with a strong family history has lipoprotein(a) measured. What is lipoprotein(a)?
opts: An HDL-like particle with apo(a) bound to apoA-I
Lipoprotein(a) is built on the LDL (low-density lipoprotein) particle and apoB-100 (apolipoprotein B-100), not on HDL (high-density lipoprotein).
A chylomicron remnant that carries apoB-48
Chylomicron remnants carry apoB-48 (apolipoprotein B-48); lipoprotein(a) carries apoB-100 plus apo(a).
An LDL-like particle with apo(a) bound to apoB-100
Correct. Lipoprotein(a) is an LDL (low-density lipoprotein)-like particle in which apo(a) (apolipoprotein(a)) is bound to apoB-100 (apolipoprotein B-100). It is more atherogenic than LDL.
A free apolipoprotein that circulates alone
It is a whole lipoprotein particle carrying cholesterol, not a free protein.

D.io: Analyze a lipid profile
D.q: A 53-year-old's report shows lipoprotein(a) and apoB (apolipoprotein B) on the same panel. Why are they reported together?
opts: Lipoprotein(a) adds to the apoB count
Correct. Each lipoprotein(a) particle carries one apoB-100 (apolipoprotein B-100), so it contributes to the total apoB particle count.
ApoB is made from lipoprotein(a)
ApoB is a structural protein made by the liver; it is not derived from lipoprotein(a).
Both are acute-phase reactants
Neither is an acute-phase reactant; C-reactive protein is, and it is made by the liver in response to inflammation.
Both are fixed genetic values
Lipoprotein(a) is largely fixed, but apoB is modifiable and followed repeatedly on therapy.

D.io: Discuss indications, advantages, and limitations of stress testing
D.q: What is obtained before an exercise stress test begins?
opts: A resting echocardiogram in every case
A resting echocardiogram is obtained for the echocardiographic stress test rather than for the standard one.
A coronary calcium score
Calcium scoring is a separate computed tomography study. What is obtained first is a resting tracing and blood pressure.
A resting electrocardiogram
Correct. Without the resting baseline there is nothing to compare the exercise tracing against. Blood pressure both supine and standing.
A radionuclide injection at rest
Resting tracer injection belongs to the nuclear perfusion study.
D.cite: Cardiac Imaging and Vascular Studies - Elwaya.pptx, Slide 33

D.io: Measure and interpret the intervals, segments and waves of the cardiac cycle
D.q: What is happening mechanically during the ST segment?
opts: The ventricles are filling during diastole
Filling corresponds to the resting portion of the cycle rather than the ST segment.
The atria are contracting
Atrial activity occurs earlier, around the P wave; the ST segment is a ventricular event.
The ventricles are repolarizing
Ventricular repolarization is the T wave, which follows the ST segment.
The ventricles are holding their contraction to allow emptying
Correct. It falls between ventricular depolarization and repolarization, and it is the part of the beat that does the ejecting.

D.io: Compare and contrast cardiovascular imaging modalities
D.q: Which combination of advantages does vascular ultrasound offer?
opts: Fast, portable, repeatable, no ionizing radiation
Correct. The combination of no radiation and easy repetition is what makes it the study you can do again tomorrow without cost to the patient. It shows both anatomy and flow.
Superior resolution to computed tomography with no operator dependence
Resolution is not its strength and it is highly operator dependent.
Reliable assessment of deep vessels regardless of body habitus
Deep vessels are harder to assess and body habitus is an explicit limitation.
Independence from the angle at which the probe is held
Probe angle can affect measurements, which is one of its limitations.
D.cite: Cardiac Imaging and Vascular Studies - Elwaya.pptx, Slide 17

D.io: Discuss diagnostic testing for: primary hemostasis, secondary hemostasis, fibrinolysis
D.q: A 53-year-old man has a fibrinogen above the reference range of 2.0 to 4.0 grams per liter. What does an elevated result indicate?
opts: Tissue damage or inflammation
Correct. Elevated fibrinogen indicates a disease involving tissue damage or inflammation.
A clotting factor deficiency
A clotting factor deficiency does not raise fibrinogen; a deficiency of fibrinogen itself lowers it. A raised level reflects tissue damage or inflammation.
Vitamin K deficiency
Vitamin K deficiency prolongs the prothrombin time and does not define an elevated fibrinogen.
Platelet dysfunction
Platelet dysfunction is assessed by function tests and is not what a raised fibrinogen signals.

D.io: Define absolute and relative refractory periods
D.q: How long does the absolute refractory period typically last?
opts: About 180 milliseconds
Correct. It runs from phase 0 to the middle of phase 3, and throughout that time the cell will not respond to another stimulus.
About 18 milliseconds
That is far too short; the absolute refractory period typically lasts about 180 milliseconds, covering phase 0 through the middle of phase 3.
About 80 milliseconds
That is too short to span phase 0 to mid phase 3; the absolute refractory period typically lasts about 180 milliseconds.
About 360 milliseconds
That is double the typical length; the absolute refractory period lasts about 180 milliseconds, ending in the middle of phase 3.

D.io: Describe measured and calculated lipid profile components
D.q: A 63-year-old's report lists non-HDL-C (non-high-density lipoprotein cholesterol). How is it derived?
opts: Total cholesterol minus triglycerides
Triglycerides are not subtracted; non-HDL-C removes only the HDL-C (high-density lipoprotein cholesterol) portion.
LDL-C minus HDL-C
Non-HDL-C starts from total cholesterol, so it includes LDL-C plus the other atherogenic particles.
Total cholesterol minus HDL-C
Correct. It captures the cholesterol in all atherogenic apoB (apolipoprotein B) lipoproteins, costs nothing extra, and is a better predictor of risk than LDL-C (low-density lipoprotein cholesterol).
HDL-C plus triglycerides divided by 5
That mixes pieces of the Friedewald equation; non-HDL-C is simply total cholesterol minus HDL-C.

D.io: Discuss indications, advantages, and limitations of echocardiography
D.q: For which of these is a transesophageal study specifically useful?
opts: Coronary artery calcium scoring
That is a non-contrast computed tomography study. The transesophageal study excels at posterior structures.
Assessing exercise capacity
Exercise capacity is assessed by stress testing rather than by an echocardiogram at rest.
Valve vegetations
Correct. All are small, posterior, or both, which is precisely where the transthoracic view falls short. Prosthetic valve function, cardiac tumors and left atrial appendage thrombus.
Measuring the cardiothoracic ratio
That is measured on a chest radiograph rather than by echocardiography.
D.cite: Cardiac Imaging and Vascular Studies - Elwaya.pptx, Slide 23

D.io: Discuss indications, advantages, and limitations of coronary angiography
D.q: A patient with an acute myocardial infarction needs the coronary arteries imaged and treated in the same procedure. Which study is appropriate?
opts: Coronary angiography
Correct. Acute infarction is a listed indication, and balloon angioplasty or stent placement can be done during the same catheter procedure.
Coronary computed tomography angiography
It assesses the coronary arteries noninvasively but cannot treat a blockage, so it cannot image and treat the vessel in one procedure.
Radionuclide perfusion imaging
It shows tracer uptake and viability but is purely diagnostic; only a catheter study can open a blocked artery during the same sitting.
Cardiovascular magnetic resonance
It shows anatomy, function and viability without radiation but offers no treatment; stent or balloon therapy needs a catheter in the coronary artery.
D.cite: Cardiac Imaging and Vascular Studies - Elwaya.pptx, Slide 72

D.io: Compare and contrast cardiac biomarkers: Creatine kinase, Cardiac troponins, BNP, hs-CRP
D.q: A 52-year-old woman's 10-year cardiovascular risk is estimated with the Reynolds Risk Score. Which biomarker does that score include?
opts: High-sensitivity cardiac troponin
Troponin is an acute injury marker and is not an input to this long-term risk score.
High-sensitivity C-reactive protein

Correct. The score estimates 10-year cardiovascular risk in women over 45 from age, systolic blood pressure, diabetes, smoking, high-density and total cholesterol, hs-CRP (high-sensitivity C-reactive protein) and a parent with myocardial infarction before 60.
B-type natriuretic peptide
The natriuretic peptides are not among the score's inputs, which pair lipids and blood pressure with an inflammatory marker.
Creatine kinase
Creatine kinase does not feature in any long-term cardiovascular risk score; its role is skeletal muscle injury.

D.io: Discuss diagnostic testing for: primary hemostasis, secondary hemostasis, fibrinolysis
D.q: A 38-year-old woman has thrombocytopenia. Which platelet index describes the uniformity of platelet size and helps with the differential diagnosis?
opts: Mean corpuscular volume
Mean corpuscular volume reports the size of red blood cells, not platelets.
Mean platelet volume
Correct. Mean platelet volume indicates the uniformity of size of the platelet population and is used for the differential diagnosis of thrombocytopenia.
Red cell distribution width
Red cell distribution width measures variation in red cell size. It says nothing about platelet size.
Bleeding time
Bleeding time measures how long a standardized skin puncture bleeds. It reflects platelet function but not platelet size.

D.io: Compare and contrast laboratory studies used to evaluate bleeding and thrombotic disorders
D.q: A 55-year-old man has a risk assessment for arterial thrombosis. Which two laboratory results are independent risk factors?
opts: Bleeding time and platelet count
These assess platelet plug formation and are not cited as independent risk factors for arterial thrombosis.
Mixing study and reptilase time
These are problem-solving tests for prolonged clotting times and not risk factors.
Prothrombin time and D-dimer
Correct. The prothrombin time and D-dimer are independent risk factors for arterial thrombosis.
Mean platelet volume and fibrin monomers
Neither is identified as an independent risk factor for arterial thrombosis.

D.io: Describe action potentials and impulse conduction through the cardiac conduction system
D.q: A cardiac cell is at minus ninety millivolts and able to respond to an impulse. Which phase is it in?
opts: Phase 0, the upstroke
The upstroke is a rapid change away from the resting voltage rather than a steady state at it.
Phase 2, the plateau
The plateau sits at a balanced voltage well above the resting level.
Phase 4, the resting state
Correct, and this is the phase in which the cell is ready and can respond, which is what distinguishes it from the refractory portion of the cycle.
Phase 3, rapid repolarization
Phase three is the return toward minus ninety rather than the steady state there.

D.io: Describe action potentials and impulse conduction through the cardiac conduction system
D.q: What two things does the atrioventricular node do to the impulse passing through it?
opts: It speeds the impulse up and attenuates it
It delays rather than accelerates, and it amplifies rather than attenuates.
It blocks every second impulse by design
Blocking alternate impulses is a pathological pattern rather than normal nodal behavior.
It introduces a short pause and amplifies the signal
Correct. The pause is what lets the atria finish emptying before the ventricles contract, so a delay in the conduction system is doing useful mechanical work.
It reverses the direction of the impulse
The impulse continues onward toward the ventricles; the node delays and amplifies it rather than reversing it.

D.io: Compare and contrast cardiac biomarkers: Creatine kinase, Cardiac troponins, BNP, hs-CRP
D.q: A 44-year-old with atypical chest pain has a measurable high-sensitivity troponin that is below the 99th percentile limit. What pitfall of the assay does this illustrate?
opts: It cannot detect small infarctions
The opposite: its added sensitivity is what allows earlier detection, including of smaller infarctions.
It cross-reacts with creatine kinase
Cross-reactivity is not the pitfall here. The problem is that it is sensitive enough to find troponin where there is no disease.
It is falsely low with obesity
Falsely low results in obesity belong to the natriuretic peptides, not to troponin.
It detects troponin in healthy people
Correct. The sensitivity is so high that measurable troponin turns up in healthy people, so the entire clinical picture has to be considered.

D.io: Determine heart rate using an electrocardiogram
D.q: What limits the use of the three hundred method?
opts: It only works on a six-second strip
The six-second requirement belongs to the other method; this one requires a regular rhythm.
It only works if the rhythm is regular
Correct, which is why regularity is assessed before rate: the answer decides which method may be used.
It only works in lead II
Lead choice is not the limitation; the method requires the rhythm to be regular.
It only works at rates above one hundred
The limitation concerns regularity rather than the rate itself.

D.io: Compare and contrast lipids and lipoproteins involved in atherosclerotic disease
D.q: A 50-year-old's lipid report mentions lipoproteins. What makes up a lipoprotein?
opts: A protein core wrapped in a triglyceride shell
The arrangement is the reverse: the lipids form the core, and the surface is phospholipid with apolipoproteins.
Free fatty acids bound to albumin alone
Albumin-bound fatty acids are not lipoproteins; a lipoprotein has a lipid core, a phospholipid shell and apolipoproteins.
Cholesterol crystals coated with fibrin
Fibrin is a clotting protein. A lipoprotein's coat is phospholipid carrying apolipoproteins.
A lipid core, phospholipid shell and apolipoproteins
Correct. The core holds cholesterol esters and triglycerides; the shell is phospholipid; the apolipoproteins are the structural and regulatory proteins on its surface.

D.io: Discuss diagnostic testing for: primary hemostasis, secondary hemostasis, fibrinolysis
D.q: A 62-year-old man has a negative fibrin monomer test. What does this result mean?
opts: Intravascular coagulation is excluded
A negative test does not exclude intravascular coagulation. A negative result can occur even when intravascular coagulation is present.
Plasmin activity is absent
Fibrin monomers reflect thrombin activity, not plasmin. A negative result says nothing definite about plasmin.
The fibrinogen level is normal
Fibrinogen is measured on its own assay, such as the Clauss method. A fibrin monomer test does not report its level.
Intravascular coagulation is not excluded
Correct. A negative fibrin monomer test does not mean intravascular coagulation is absent; a positive one indicates thrombin activity.

D.io: Interpret common coagulation studies including: PT, INR, aPTT, D-dimer
D.q: A 64-year-old man has blood drawn at two hospitals, each with a different reagent. Why is the international normalized ratio reported?
opts: It measures platelet function
Platelet function is tested by aggregometry or platelet function analysis, not by the international normalized ratio.
It measures fibrin breakdown
Fibrin breakdown is evaluated by D-dimer and related products. The international normalized ratio comes from the prothrombin time.
It replaces the partial thromboplastin time
The two tests assess different pathways. The international normalized ratio standardizes only the prothrombin time.
It standardizes the prothrombin time
Correct. Across laboratories, the international normalized ratio adjusts the prothrombin time ratio so results can be standardized from laboratory to laboratory.

D.io: Discuss indications for ordering a lipid profile
D.q: A healthy 30-year-old asks why a lipid profile is being ordered at his first visit. Which is an indication?
opts: Ruling out an acute infarction
Acute infarction is ruled out with serial troponin; lipids answer the long-term risk question.
Triage of acute dyspnea
Acute dyspnea triage for suspected heart failure uses a natriuretic peptide.
Baseline and risk estimation
Correct. A lipid profile is indicated for baseline documentation, atherosclerotic risk estimation, and guiding and monitoring lipid-lowering therapy in nearly all adults.
Screening for muscle injury
Muscle injury is evaluated with creatine kinase; a lipid profile answers long-term atherosclerotic risk instead.

D.io: Define depolarization and repolarization
D.q: What does depolarization represent, and what is its relationship to contraction?
opts: Recovery of cardiac tissue, and it follows contraction
Recovery is repolarization; depolarization is activation and it comes before contraction.
Activation of cardiac tissue, and it precedes contraction
Correct, and the order matters: the electrical event comes first, so an electrocardiogram showing depolarization does not prove the muscle actually contracted.
Activation of cardiac tissue, occurring simultaneously with contraction
The activation precedes the contraction rather than coinciding with it.
The resting state of the cell between beats
The resting state is phase four, which is neither depolarization nor repolarization.

D.io: Describe measured and calculated lipid profile components
D.q: A 47-year-old's panel shows triglycerides of 480 mg/dL (desirable below 150 mg/dL). What is true of a Friedewald LDL-C (low-density lipoprotein cholesterol) on this sample?
opts: It cannot be used
Correct. The Friedewald equation cannot be used when triglycerides are 400 mg/dL or above. The Martin/Hopkins and Sampson/NIH (National Institutes of Health) equations are now preferred.
It is the most accurate estimate
At this triglyceride level Friedewald is invalid, and newer equations are preferred for greater accuracy even below it.
It is falsely high but usable
The equation is not merely biased at this level; it cannot be used at all once triglycerides reach 400 mg/dL.
It becomes a direct measurement
Friedewald is always a calculation; it never becomes a measurement.

D.io: Discuss indications, advantages, and limitations of cardiac CT
D.q: Why are cardiac medications given before a cardiac computed tomography study?
opts: To dilate the coronary arteries so contrast reaches the myocardium
Rate control is the stated reason, together with electrocardiographic synchronization.
To prevent an allergic reaction to the contrast
Premedication for contrast allergy is not what is described here.
To provoke ischemia during the scan
Provoking ischemia is what a stress test does; the medication here steadies the heart.
To control heart rate, since the moving heart degrades the images
Correct, and the study is also synchronized to an electrocardiogram so the heart can be examined at chosen points in the cycle.
D.cite: Cardiac Imaging and Vascular Studies - Elwaya.pptx, Slide 41

D.io: Identify common abnormal cardiovascular imaging findings
D.q: How are veins and arteries told apart on a vascular ultrasound?
opts: Veins pulsate and arteries collapse when compressed
The behaviors are the other way round: veins collapse under compression and arteries pulsate.
Veins collapse when compressed and arteries pulsate
Correct. Compression is the maneuver the whole deep vein thrombosis study rests on, because a vein that will not collapse has something in it.
Veins appear bright and arteries appear dark
Both appear as well circumscribed hypoechoic or anechoic structures.
Only Doppler can distinguish them
Compression and pulsatility distinguish them on gray scale alone.
D.cite: Cardiac Imaging and Vascular Studies - Elwaya.pptx, Slide 15

D.io: Discuss indications for ordering cardiac biomarkers
D.q: A 69-year-old with new exertional dyspnea has a B-type natriuretic peptide below the assay's heart failure cutoff. How is that result used?
opts: To rule in acute myocardial infarction
Infarction is diagnosed with troponin. A natriuretic peptide reflects stretch, not injury.
To rule out new-onset heart failure
Correct. The natriuretic peptides can serve as a rule-out test for suspected new-onset heart failure, used together with the clinical assessment and an echocardiogram if indicated.
To confirm heart failure on its own
Neither peptide is 100% specific for heart failure, and neither is meant to be a stand-alone test.
To estimate long-term atherosclerotic risk
Long-term atherosclerotic risk comes from the lipid profile and risk markers such as high-sensitivity C-reactive protein.

D.io: Discuss diagnostic testing for: primary hemostasis, secondary hemostasis, fibrinolysis
D.q: A 60-year-old man on heparin has a prolonged thrombin time. Which test stays normal, pointing to heparin rather than a fibrinogen defect?
opts: Reptilase time
Correct. The reptilase time is normal with heparin because it mainly assesses fibrinogen function, separating heparin effect from a fibrinogen problem.
Activated partial thromboplastin time
Heparin prolongs the activated partial thromboplastin time, so it does not stay normal.
D-dimer
D-dimer marks fibrin breakdown and does not distinguish heparin from a fibrinogen defect.
Mean platelet volume
Mean platelet volume describes platelet size and plays no part in separating these causes.

D.io: Describe laboratory findings associated with platelet abnormalities
D.q: A 33-year-old woman has thrombocytopenia, and her smear shows fragmented red blood cells. What are these fragments called?
opts: Schistocytes
Correct. The smear in thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura shows red cell fragments, called schistocytes, in addition to the thrombocytopenia.
Target cells
Target cells have a central dark spot and are not fragments. They are not the finding in thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura.
Spherocytes
Spherocytes are small dense round red cells that lack central pallor. Fragmented, helmet-shaped cells are schistocytes.
Teardrop cells
Teardrop cells have a single tapered tail. The fragmented cells of thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura are schistocytes.

D.io: Describe action potentials and impulse conduction through the cardiac conduction system
D.q: What is distinctive about the bundle of His in a normal heart?
opts: It is one of several pathways crossing the atrioventricular junction
In a normal heart it is the only one; additional pathways are abnormal.
It paces the heart at sixty to a hundred beats per minute
That intrinsic rate belongs to the sinoatrial node; the bundle of His is a conducting pathway rather than a pacemaker.
It lies within the atrial wall
It connects the atrioventricular node to the bundle branches across the nonconductive wall between the chambers.
It is the only electrical pathway crossing from the atria to the ventricles
Correct. Everything above and below has to go through it, which is why a block there separates the two halves of the heart electrically.

D.io: Describe action potentials and impulse conduction through the cardiac conduction system
D.q: Which property refers to a cardiac cell's ability to produce its own impulse?
opts: Automaticity
Correct. It is why the heart beats without instruction from anywhere else, and why several parts of it can take over pacemaking if the one above fails.
Excitability
Excitability is the ability to respond to an impulse or stimulus rather than to generate one.
Conductivity
Conductivity is the ability to pass an impulse from one myocyte to the next.
Contractility
Contractility is the ability of the cell to shorten, which is the mechanical consequence rather than the electrical origin.

E.io: Compare and contrast cardiac biomarkers: Creatine kinase, Cardiac troponins, BNP, hs-CRP
E.q: A 45-year-old has a C-reactive protein checked during an acute infection and again after recovery. How does the level behave?
opts: It rises slowly and stays high for years
C-reactive protein responds fast in both directions; it does not linger once the inflammation resolves.
It rises quickly and drops rapidly
Correct. C-reactive protein is an acute-phase reactant from the liver: it rises quickly in response to inflammation and drops rapidly once the process resolves.
It stays constant throughout life
A lifetime-stable, genetically set value describes lipoprotein(a), not C-reactive protein.
It falls during active infection
Infection raises C-reactive protein, and bacterial infections produce the highest levels.

E.io: Compare and contrast lipids and lipoproteins involved in atherosclerotic disease
E.q: A 60-year-old asks why VLDL (very low-density lipoprotein) remnants and LDL (low-density lipoprotein) all count toward plaque. What do they share?
opts: Each carries apoA-I and removes cholesterol from the wall
Carrying apoA-I (apolipoprotein A-I) and removing cholesterol describes HDL (high-density lipoprotein), which performs reverse cholesterol transport.
Each is an apoB particle small enough to enter the artery wall

Correct. Each apoB (apolipoprotein B) particle under about 70 nm can cross the endothelium and become trapped in the artery wall, initiating plaque. That is why therapy aims to reduce the number of circulating apoB particles.
Each is made in the intestine from dietary fat after meals
Intestinal particles from dietary fat are chylomicrons, on apoB-48 (apolipoprotein B-48); VLDL and LDL come from the liver.
Each is too large to cross the endothelium into the wall
The opposite: particles under about 70 nm can cross the endothelial barrier, and that is how plaque begins.

E.io: Discuss indications, advantages, and limitations of echocardiography
E.q: Which esophageal conditions contraindicate a transesophageal echocardiogram?
opts: Gastroesophageal reflux disease
Reflux alone is not listed. Stricture, malignancy and bleeding varices are the esophageal contraindications.
A history of esophageal candidiasis
Not among the listed contraindications, which are stricture, malignancy and varices with recent or active bleeding.
Stricture, malignancy or bleeding varices
Correct. All three mean passing a probe risks perforation or hemorrhage, which is the hazard the contraindication list exists to avoid.
Recent barium swallow
Not among the listed contraindications; stricture, malignancy and bleeding varices are the esophageal ones.
E.cite: Cardiac Imaging and Vascular Studies - Elwaya.pptx, Slide 26

E.io: Discuss indications, advantages, and limitations of echocardiography
E.q: Why is a transesophageal study used in a patient presenting with cerebral ischemia?
opts: It measures cerebral blood flow directly and noninvasively
Echocardiography images the heart rather than the cerebral circulation.
It assesses the carotid arteries
The carotids are assessed by vascular ultrasound. The transesophageal study looks for a cardiac source of embolus.
It can find thrombus in the left atrial appendage
Correct. It looks for the source rather than the consequence, and the appendage is the site the transthoracic study sees worst.
It excludes coronary stenosis
Coronary stenosis is not assessed by echocardiography; it needs computed tomography angiography or catheter angiography.
E.cite: Cardiac Imaging and Vascular Studies - Elwaya.pptx, Slide 23

E.io: Define absolute and relative refractory periods
E.q: Over which part of the action potential does the ABSOLUTE refractory period run?
opts: From the middle of phase 3 to the end of phase 3
That span is the RELATIVE refractory period, in which a strong enough stimulus can succeed.
Throughout phase 4
Phase four is the resting state, in which the cell is ready to respond rather than refractory.
From phase 0 to the middle of phase 3
Correct, and it lasts about a hundred and eighty milliseconds, during which no stimulus of any strength will produce another action potential.
From phase 1 to phase 2 only
The absolute period begins at the upstroke and extends well past the plateau.

E.io: Discuss the use of lipid testing for cardiovascular risk assessment
E.q: A 56-year-old has just started a statin. When should the lipid panel be rechecked?
opts: In 4 to 12 weeks
Correct. Check lipids 4 to 12 weeks after starting or changing the dose of lipid-lowering therapy, then every 6 to 12 months.
In 5 years
Five-yearly is the routine adult screening interval, not the recheck after starting therapy.
In 1 week
One week is too early to judge the response; the recheck comes at 4 to 12 weeks after starting.
Only if he has symptoms
Monitoring is scheduled, not symptom-driven: 4 to 12 weeks, then every 6 to 12 months.

E.io: Compare and contrast cardiac biomarkers: Creatine kinase, Cardiac troponins, BNP, hs-CRP
E.q: A 57-year-old man's chart lists a high-sensitivity troponin. What does the term high-sensitivity describe?
opts: A fourth troponin subunit
There are three troponin subunits, T, I and C. High-sensitivity refers to the assay, not to a new protein.
A skeletal muscle troponin
It measures cardiac troponin I or T, just at lower concentrations. It is not a marker for skeletal muscle.
The assay's characteristics
Correct. It is not a different subunit of troponin. The assay detects circulating troponin at lower concentrations, which is where its advantage comes from.
A troponin corrected for age
Nothing about the name refers to age adjustment. Whether limits should be age-matched is a separate, still-debated question.

E.io: Describe the fundamental principles of electrocardiography
E.q: No calipers are available and a rhythm may be irregular. What is the most appropriate way to compare consecutive R to R intervals?
opts: A count of complexes in three seconds
A raw count gives a rate, not a comparison of consecutive R to R intervals; without calipers, a marked sheet of paper is used for regularity.
The three hundred method on one interval
That method gives a rate and only works if the rhythm is already regular, so it cannot test regularity; a marked sheet of paper can.
A marked sheet of paper
Correct. Marking two R waves on a paper edge and sliding it along the strip does the job of calipers for comparing consecutive R to R intervals.
The QT interval between two beats
The QT interval measures ventricular activity within one beat and says nothing about spacing between beats; a marked sheet of paper compares R to R intervals.

E.io: Measure and interpret the intervals, segments and waves of the cardiac cycle
E.q: What does the P wave represent, and how should it appear in lead II?
opts: Atrial repolarization, appearing as a negative deflection
Atrial repolarization is not what the P wave represents, and in lead II it is upright.
Ventricular depolarization, appearing as a positive deflection
Ventricular depolarization is the QRS complex rather than the P wave, which is atrial.
Atrial depolarization, appearing as a positive deflection
Correct, with a normal duration under three small boxes, and it is the first upward deflection before the QRS complex.
The resting state between beats
The resting state corresponds to the TP segment rather than to a wave.

E.io: Discuss indications, advantages, and limitations of cardiac CT
E.q: What advantages does cardiac computed tomography have over echocardiography?
opts: Superior resolution and noninvasive coronary assessment
Correct, with fast acquisition and interpretation as well, which together make it the anatomical study of choice. It also shows internal structures directly, and acquires and reports quickly.
Assessment of cardiac function as well as anatomy
Function is exactly what it cannot assess; that is left to echocardiography and magnetic resonance.
Freedom from ionizing radiation
Radiation is one of its disadvantages rather than an advantage; magnetic resonance is what avoids it.
Independence from heart rate and rhythm
It is rhythm and rate dependent, which is why rate control is given beforehand.
E.cite: Cardiac Imaging and Vascular Studies - Elwaya.pptx, Slide 44

E.io: Compare and contrast lipids and lipoproteins involved in atherosclerotic disease
E.q: A 55-year-old asks how LDL (low-density lipoprotein) forms in the circulation. What is the sequence?
opts: HDL gains triglyceride, becoming a remnant, then LDL
HDL (high-density lipoprotein) carries apolipoprotein A-I and has no apolipoprotein B; it is not the precursor of LDL.
VLDL loses triglyceride, becoming a remnant, then LDL

Correct. The liver secretes triglyceride-rich VLDL (very low-density lipoprotein); lipoprotein lipase strips triglyceride to give a remnant (IDL, intermediate-density lipoprotein) and then cholesterol-rich LDL. It is the same apolipoprotein B particle at different stages.
Chylomicrons gain cholesterol in the liver, then LDL
Chylomicrons carry dietary triglyceride on apolipoprotein B-48; LDL comes from hepatic VLDL (very low-density lipoprotein) on apolipoprotein B-100.
LDL loses cholesterol, becoming a remnant, then VLDL
The direction is reversed: VLDL (very low-density lipoprotein) comes first and loses triglyceride to become LDL.

E.io: Describe laboratory findings associated with platelet abnormalities
E.q: A 31-year-old man has thrombocytopenia, and his smear shows inclusions inside neutrophils. Which disorder fits?
opts: May-Hegglin anomaly
Correct. Neutrophil inclusions on the smear point to May-Hegglin anomaly, a myosin heavy chain 9 disorder, among the morphologic causes of platelet abnormality.
Gray platelet syndrome
Gray platelet syndrome features large, pale gray platelets rather than neutrophil inclusions.
Immune thrombocytopenia
Immune thrombocytopenia has a low count but no characteristic neutrophil inclusions.
Hemophilia B
Hemophilia B is a factor IX deficiency with a prolonged partial thromboplastin time and normal platelet morphology.

E.io: Interpret common coagulation studies including: PT, INR, aPTT, D-dimer
E.q: A 33-year-old woman has calf cramping and a low suspicion of thrombosis. In which situation does a D-dimer add the most value?
opts: When a normal result is expected
Correct. D-dimer is most useful for its negative predictive value: a normal result helps exclude thrombosis, so it adds value only when a normal result is plausible.
When a clot is already known to be present
A raised D-dimer is expected when a clot is known to exist, so it adds no new information.
When the clot location is needed
D-dimer is nonspecific and does not show where a clot is. Imaging locates it.
When platelet function is in doubt
Platelet function is evaluated by aggregometry or platelet function analysis, not D-dimer.

E.io: Compare and contrast cardiac biomarkers: Creatine kinase, Cardiac troponins, BNP, hs-CRP
E.q: A 50-year-old with a body mass index of 44 has orthopnea and edema, yet a B-type natriuretic peptide below the heart failure cutoff. What explains the discrepancy?
opts: Obesity falsely lowers natriuretic peptides
Correct. A high body mass index is associated with falsely low natriuretic peptide levels, so a normal-looking value does not reassure in this patient.
Obesity falsely raises natriuretic peptides
The direction is the other way: obesity suppresses the natriuretic peptides.
Obesity makes troponin falsely positive
The pitfall of obesity belongs to the natriuretic peptides, which it lowers, not to troponin.
Obesity makes the assay invalid entirely
The assay is still valid; obesity shifts the value downward, which is why interpretation has to account for it.

E.io: Identify the standard limb and precordial leads and their proper anatomical placement
E.q: What are contiguous leads?
opts: Leads placed physically next to one another on the skin
The grouping is by the region of heart viewed rather than by skin position.
Two or more leads looking at the same area of the heart
Correct, which is why a change appearing in a contiguous group means more than the same change in one isolated lead.
Leads that share a single physical electrode
Sharing an electrode is not what defines a contiguous group.
Leads recorded at the same moment in time
All leads are recorded together; contiguity refers to the area viewed.

E.io: Interpret common coagulation studies including: PT, INR, aPTT, D-dimer
E.q: A 49-year-old man not on warfarin has an international normalized ratio of 2.6 (reference 0.8 to 1.2). Which cause fits?
opts: Immune thrombocytopenia
Immune thrombocytopenia lowers the platelet count and leaves the prothrombin time normal.
Liver disease
Correct. Off warfarin, an abnormal prothrombin time or international normalized ratio may indicate a bleeding disorder, a clotting disorder, liver disease or vitamin K deficiency.
Hemophilia A
Hemophilia A prolongs the partial thromboplastin time and leaves the prothrombin time normal.
Acute thrombosis
Acute thrombosis typically shows a raised D-dimer with a normal prothrombin time.

E.io: Measure and interpret the intervals, segments and waves of the cardiac cycle
E.q: What does the Q wave represent, and why is it negative in lead II?
opts: Depolarization of the anterior left ventricle, traveling toward lead II
That is the R wave, and traveling toward the lead is why it is positive.
Depolarization of the lateral wall of the left ventricle
That is the S wave, which like the Q wave travels away from lead II and so deflects downward.
Repolarization of the ventricles
Ventricular repolarization is the T wave rather than any part of the QRS complex.
Depolarization of the interventricular septum, which travels away from lead II
Correct. The direction of that particular wavefront is what makes the deflection downward, and it is not always visible.

E.io: Discuss indications for ordering cardiac biomarkers
E.q: A 61-year-old man has had crushing chest pain with diaphoresis for 40 minutes. Which biomarker testing is first-line?
opts: A single creatine kinase level
Creatine kinase is largely historical for myocardial infarction and has low cardiac specificity. Troponin replaced it wherever troponin is available.
Serial myoglobin levels
Myoglobin is on the list of markers no longer used to evaluate cardiac disease. It adds no diagnostic value once troponin is available.
Serial high-sensitivity troponin
Correct. Serial values are the point: a rising or falling pattern identifies acute injury, and the initial troponin also carries prognostic weight in acute coronary syndrome.
High-sensitivity C-reactive protein
High-sensitivity C-reactive protein is a long-term risk marker for atherosclerotic disease, explicitly not a test for an acute cardiac event.

E.io: Describe the fundamental principles of electrocardiography
E.q: Reading left to right across the paper measures time. What does reading up and down measure?
opts: Rate
Rate is derived from how many complexes occupy a span of time along the horizontal axis.
Voltage
Correct, and at standard calibration a small box is a tenth of a millivolt, with a ten millimeter deflection equal to one millivolt.
Time in a second dimension
Time runs along the horizontal axis only; the vertical axis measures voltage.
Conduction velocity
Velocity is not read from the vertical axis, which measures voltage in millivolts.

E.io: Compare and contrast lipids and lipoproteins involved in atherosclerotic disease
E.q: A 57-year-old has an apoB (apolipoprotein B) level measured. Which particles carry apoB-100 (apolipoprotein B-100)?
opts: Chylomicrons and HDL only
Chylomicrons carry apoB-48 (apolipoprotein B-48), and HDL (high-density lipoprotein) carries no apoB at all.
HDL, VLDL and chylomicrons
HDL (high-density lipoprotein) has no apoB, and chylomicrons carry the intestinal apoB-48 form.
VLDL, IDL, LDL and lipoprotein(a)
Correct. ApoB-100 is synthesized by the liver and found on very low-density, intermediate-density and low-density lipoprotein and on lipoprotein(a), one per particle.
Lipoprotein(a) and HDL only
Lipoprotein(a) does carry apoB-100, but HDL (high-density lipoprotein) does not; it is built on apoA-I (apolipoprotein A-I).

E.io: Discuss indications, advantages, and limitations of nuclear cardiology studies
E.q: On what principle does radionuclide myocardial perfusion imaging work?
opts: Diseased myocardium takes up more tracer than normal myocardium
Uptake is reduced rather than increased where flow is reduced.
Tracer is taken up only by scarred tissue
Uptake marks functional, viable tissue; scar does not take it up.
The tracer is metabolized into a contrast agent within the coronary arteries
The tracer emits gamma rays that the camera detects rather than becoming contrast.
Under stress, diseased myocardium receives less blood flow than normal myocardium
Correct, so comparing stress images against rest images is what makes the difference visible rather than either set alone.
